questions.question: How much does increasing a receiver’s bandwidth from 50 Hz to 1,000 Hz increase the receiver’s noise floor?
questions.explanation: Noise power scales with bandwidth: 10 log(1000/50) = 10 log(20) ≈ 13 dB.

questions.question: What does the MDS of a receiver represent?
questions.explanation: MDS is the minimum discernible signal: the input level that just equals the noise floor (3 dB above noise) in a stated bandwidth.

questions.question: An SDR receiver is overloaded when input signals exceed what level?
answers: One-half of the maximum sample rate
One-half of the maximum sampling buffer size
The maximum count value of the analog-to-digital converter
The reference voltage of the analog-to-digital converter
questions.explanation: When the input exceeds the ADC's reference voltage (its full-scale range), the samples clip and the receiver is overloaded.

questions.question: Which of the following choices is a good reason for selecting a high IF for a superheterodyne HF or VHF communications receiver?
answers: Easier for front-end circuitry to eliminate image responses
questions.explanation: With a high IF, the image frequency (2 × IF away from the desired signal) lies far away, so simple front-end filters can reject it.

questions.question: What is an advantage of having a variety of receiver bandwidths from which to select?
answers: The noise figure of the RF amplifier can be adjusted to match the modulation type, thus increasing receiver sensitivity
Receiver power consumption can be reduced when wider bandwidth is not required
Receive bandwidth can be set to match the modulation bandwidth, maximizing signal-to-noise ratio and minimizing interference
Multiple frequencies can be received simultaneously if desired
questions.explanation: Matching the receive bandwidth to the signal (for example 500 Hz for CW, 2.4 kHz for SSB) lets in the least noise and adjacent-signal interference, which gives the best SNR.

questions.question: Why does input attenuation reduce receiver overload on the lower frequency HF bands with little or no impact on signal-to-noise ratio?
answers: The attenuator has a low-pass filter to increase the strength of lower frequency signals
The attenuator has a noise filter to suppress interference
Signals are attenuated separately from the noise
Atmospheric noise is generally greater than internally generated noise even after attenuation
questions.explanation: On the lower HF bands, atmospheric noise is far above the receiver's own noise. An attenuator lowers the signal and the band noise equally, so SNR barely changes while overload goes down.

questions.question: How does a narrow-band roofing filter affect receiver performance?
answers: It improves sensitivity by reducing front-end noise
It improves intelligibility by using low Q circuitry to reduce ringing
It improves blocking dynamic range by attenuating strong signals near the receive frequency
questions.explanation: A roofing filter sits right after the first mixer and passes only a narrow band. It keeps strong nearby signals out of the later stages, which improves blocking dynamic range.

questions.question: What is reciprocal mixing?
answers: Two out-of-band signals mixing to generate an in-band spurious signal
In-phase signals cancelling in a mixer resulting in loss of receiver sensitivity
Two digital signals combining from alternate time slots
Local oscillator phase noise mixing with adjacent strong signals to create interference to desired signals
questions.explanation: Reciprocal mixing is LO phase noise mixing with strong adjacent signals, which spreads noise across the desired channel.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the receiver IF Shift control?
answers: To permit listening on a different frequency from the transmitting frequency
To reduce interference from stations transmitting on adjacent frequencies
To tune in stations slightly off frequency without changing the transmit frequency
questions.explanation: IF shift moves the IF passband relative to the signal, so you can move an adjacent interfering signal outside the filter without retuning.

questions.question: What is meant by the blocking dynamic range of a receiver?
answers: The difference in dB between the noise floor and the level of an incoming signal that will cause 1 dB of gain compression
The minimum difference in dB between the levels of two FM signals that will cause one signal to block the other
The difference in dB between the noise floor and the third-order intercept point
The minimum difference in dB between two signals which produce third-order intermodulation products greater than the noise floor
questions.explanation: Blocking dynamic range runs from the noise floor (MDS) up to the level of an off-frequency signal that causes 1 dB of gain compression.

questions.question: Which of the following describes problems caused by poor dynamic range in a receiver?
answers: Spurious signals caused by cross modulation and desensitization from strong adjacent signals
Oscillator instability requiring frequent retuning and loss of ability to recover the opposite sideband
Poor weak signal reception caused by insufficient local oscillator injection
Oscillator instability and severe audio distortion of all but the strongest received signals
questions.explanation: A receiver with poor dynamic range lets strong signals cause cross-modulation and desensitization. That produces false signals and loss of weak ones.

questions.question: What creates intermodulation interference between two repeaters in close proximity?
answers: The output signals cause feedback in the final amplifier of one or both transmitters
The output signals mix in the final amplifier of one or both transmitters
The input frequencies are harmonically related
The output frequencies are harmonically related
questions.explanation: When two repeater transmitters couple into each other's final amplifiers, the nonlinear finals mix the signals and transmit IMD products.

questions.question: Which of the following is used to reduce or eliminate intermodulation interference in a repeater caused by a nearby transmitter?
answers: A band-pass filter in the feed line between the transmitter and receiver
A properly terminated circulator at the output of the repeater’s transmitter
Utilizing a Class C final amplifier
Utilizing a Class D final amplifier
questions.explanation: A circulator (an isolator when its third port is terminated) passes the transmitter's power out to the antenna but blocks signals coming back from a nearby transmitter. That prevents mixing in the final.

questions.question: What is the term for the reduction in receiver sensitivity caused by a strong signal near the received frequency?
questions.explanation: Desensitization (blocking) is the drop in sensitivity caused by a strong nearby signal driving the front end into compression or AGC.

questions.question: Which of the following reduces the likelihood of receiver desensitization?
answers: Insert attenuation before the first RF stage
Switch from fast AGC to slow AGC
questions.explanation: Attenuation ahead of the first RF stage lowers the strong signal enough to keep the front end linear, which reduces desensitization.

questions.question: What causes intermodulation in an electronic circuit?
questions.explanation: Intermodulation happens only in nonlinear devices. A nonlinear transfer curve creates sum and difference products of the input signals.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the preselector in a communications receiver?
answers: To store frequencies that are often used
To provide broadband attenuation before the first RF stage to prevent intermodulation
To increase the rejection of signals outside the band being received
To allow selection of the optimum RF amplifier device
questions.explanation: A preselector is a tunable front-end filter. It rejects strong signals outside the band being received.

questions.question: What does a third-order intercept level of 40 dBm mean with respect to receiver performance?
answers: Signals less than 40 dBm will not generate audible third-order intermodulation products
The receiver can tolerate signals up to 40 dB above the noise floor without producing third-order intermodulation products
A pair of 40 dBm input signals will theoretically generate a third-order intermodulation product that has the same output amplitude as either of the input signals
A pair of 1 mW input signals will produce a third-order intermodulation product that is 40 dB stronger than the input signal
questions.explanation: The third-order intercept is the theoretical point where the IMD products would equal the desired signals in level. An IP3 of +40 dBm means two +40 dBm inputs would produce IMD equal to either one.

questions.question: Why are odd-order intermodulation products, created within a receiver, of particular interest compared to other products?
answers: Odd-order products of two signals in the band being received are also likely to be within the band
Odd-order products are more likely to overload the IF filters
Odd-order products are an indication of poor image rejection
Odd-order intermodulation produces three products for every input signal within the band of interest
questions.explanation: Third-order products such as 2f1 − f2 fall close to the original signals, often inside the same band, so a filter cannot easily remove them.

questions.question: What is the link margin in a system with a transmit power level of 10 W (+40 dBm), a system antenna gain of 10 dBi, a cable loss of 3 dB, a path loss of 136 dB, a receiver minimum discernable signal of -103 dBm, and a required signal-to-noise ratio of 6 dB?
questions.explanation: Received level = 40 + 10 − 3 − 136 = −89 dBm. The required level is MDS + SNR = −103 + 6 = −97 dBm, so the link margin is −89 − (−97) = +8 dB.

questions.question: What is the received signal level with a transmit power of 10 W (+40 dBm), a transmit antenna gain of 6 dBi, a receive antenna gain of 3 dBi, and a path loss of 100 dB?
questions.explanation: Received level = 40 + 6 + 3 − 100 = −51 dBm.

questions.question: What power level does a receiver minimum discernible signal of -100 dBm represent?
What problem can occur when using an automatic notch filter (ANF) to remove interfering carriers while receiving CW signals?
answers: Removal of the CW signal as well as the interfering carrier
Any nearby signal passing through the DSP system will overwhelm the desired signal
questions.explanation: An automatic notch filter attacks steady tones, and a CW signal is a steady carrier, so the ANF can notch out the signal you want.

questions.question: Which of the following types of noise can often be reduced by a digital noise reduction?
questions.explanation: DSP noise reduction can reduce random (white) noise and many repetitive noises such as ignition and power-line noise. All the choices are correct.

questions.question: Which of the following types of noise are removed by a noise blanker?
questions.explanation: A noise blanker gates off the receiver during short, strong pulses. It works on impulse noise only.

questions.question: How can conducted noise from an automobile battery charging system be suppressed?
answers: By installing filter capacitors in series with the alternator leads
By installing a noise suppression resistor and a blocking capacitor at the battery
By installing a high-pass filter in series with the radio’s power lead and a low-pass filter in parallel with the antenna feed line
By installing ferrite chokes on the charging system leads
questions.explanation: Ferrite chokes on the charging leads present a high impedance to RF noise currents, which suppresses conducted alternator whine and noise.

questions.question: What is used to suppress radio frequency interference from a line-driven AC motor?
answers: A high-pass filter in series with the motor’s power leads
A brute-force AC-line filter in series with the motor’s power leads
A bypass capacitor in series with the motor’s field winding
A bypass choke in parallel with the motor’s field winding
questions.explanation: A brute-force AC line filter (LC low-pass) in series with the motor leads keeps RF noise from being conducted onto the wiring and radiated.

questions.question: What type of electrical interference can be caused by computer network equipment?
answers: A loud AC hum in the audio output of your station’s receiver
A clicking noise at intervals of a few seconds
The appearance of unstable modulated or unmodulated signals at specific frequencies
A whining-type noise that continually pulses off and on
questions.explanation: Ethernet and network gear can radiate clock and data harmonics. They show up as unstable or warbling signals on specific frequencies.

questions.question: Which of the following can cause shielded cables to radiate or receive interference?
answers: Low inductance ground connections at both ends of the shield
Common-mode currents on the shield and conductors
Tying all ground connections to a common point resulting in differential-mode currents in the shield
questions.explanation: Common-mode current on the outside of the shield and conductors, often from poor terminations or ground loops, makes the cable act as an antenna.

questions.question: What current flows equally on all conductors of an unshielded multiconductor cable?
questions.explanation: Common-mode current flows equally and in the same direction on all conductors. Differential-mode current flows out on one conductor and back on another.

questions.question: What undesirable effect can occur when using a noise blanker?
answers: Received audio in the speech range might have an echo effect
The audio frequency bandwidth of the received signal might be compressed
Strong signals may be distorted and appear to cause spurious emissions
FM signals can no longer be demodulated
questions.explanation: When strong signals are present, the noise blanker's gating can chop them up. The result is IMD-like distortion and false signals.

questions.question: Which of the following can create intermittent loud roaring or buzzing AC line interference?
answers: Arcing contacts in a thermostatically controlled device
A defective doorbell or doorbell transformer inside a nearby residence
questions.explanation: Arcing thermostat contacts, faulty doorbell transformers and failing neon or illuminated signs can all produce intermittent roaring or buzzing line noise. All the choices are correct.

questions.question: What could be the cause of local AM broadcast band signals combining to generate spurious signals on the MF or HF bands?
answers: One or more of the broadcast stations is transmitting an over-modulated signal
Nearby corroded metal connections are mixing and reradiating the broadcast signals
You are receiving skywave signals from a distant station
Your station receiver IF amplifier stage is overloaded
questions.explanation: Corroded joints (the "rusty bolt effect") act as nonlinear diodes. They mix strong AM broadcast signals and reradiate the products on other frequencies.

questions.question: What causes interference received as a series of carriers at regular intervals across a wide frequency range?
questions.explanation: Switch-mode power supplies switch at a fixed rate and radiate harmonics. These appear as a series of carriers at regular intervals across a wide range.

questions.question: Where should a station AC surge protector be installed?
answers: On the single point ground panel
On a ground rod outside the station
questions.explanation: Bonding the surge protector at the single-point ground panel keeps every protected line at the same potential during a surge.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a single point ground panel?
answers: Remove AC power in case of a short-circuit
Prevent common-mode transients in multi-wire systems
Eliminate air gaps between protected and non-protected circuits
Ensure all lightning protectors activate at the same time
questions.explanation: With everything bonded at one panel, all protectors reference the same point and fire together. That avoids potential differences between lines during a lightning strike.
questions.explanationNote: Rationale follows the pool answer key; real-world purpose is more broadly equalizing potentials.

questions.question: What can cause the voltage across reactances in a series RLC circuit to be higher than the voltage applied to the entire circuit?
questions.explanation: At series resonance, XL and XC cancel and the current is limited only by R. The large current through each reactance produces voltages of Q times the applied voltage across L and across C.

questions.question: What is the resonant frequency of an RLC circuit if R is 22 ohms, L is 50 microhenries, and C is 40 picofarads?
questions.explanation: f = 1/(2π√(LC)) = 1/(2π√(50×10⁻⁶ × 40×10⁻¹²)) = 1/(2π × 4.47×10⁻⁸) ≈ 3.56 MHz. R does not affect the resonant frequency.

questions.question: What is the magnitude of the impedance of a series RLC circuit at resonance?
answers: High, compared to the circuit resistance
questions.explanation: At resonance, XL = XC and they cancel, so a series RLC circuit's impedance is just R, its minimum.

questions.question: What is the magnitude of the impedance of a parallel RLC circuit at resonance?
answers: Low compared to the circuit resistance
High compared to the circuit resistance
questions.explanation: At parallel resonance the L and C branch currents cancel. The tank looks like an open circuit, so the impedance is set by the resistance: maximum and purely resistive.

questions.question: What is the result of increasing the Q of an impedance-matching circuit?
questions.explanation: Bandwidth = f/Q, so raising the Q of a matching network narrows the range of frequencies over which it gives a good match.

questions.question: What is the magnitude of the circulating current within the components of a parallel LC circuit at resonance?
answers: It equals 1 divided by the quantity 2 times pi, times the square root of (inductance L multiplied by capacitance C)
It equals 2 times pi, times the square root of (inductance L multiplied by capacitance C)
questions.explanation: At resonance in a parallel LC tank, energy sloshes between L and C. The circulating current is at its maximum, about Q times the line current.

questions.question: What is the magnitude of the current at the input of a parallel RLC circuit at resonance?
questions.explanation: A parallel RLC circuit's impedance is at its maximum at resonance, so the current drawn from the source is at its minimum.

questions.question: What is the phase relationship between the current through and the voltage across a series resonant circuit at resonance?
answers: The voltage leads the current by 90 degrees
The current leads the voltage by 90 degrees
The voltage and current are in phase
The voltage and current are 180 degrees out of phase
questions.explanation: At series resonance the reactances cancel and the circuit is purely resistive, so voltage and current are in phase.

questions.question: How is the Q of an RLC parallel resonant circuit calculated?
answers: Reactance of either the inductance or capacitance divided by the resistance
Reactance of either the inductance or capacitance multiplied by the resistance
Resistance divided by the reactance of either the inductance or capacitance
Reactance of the inductance multiplied by the reactance of the capacitance
questions.explanation: For a parallel resonant circuit, Q = R / X, where X is either XL or XC (they are equal at resonance). For a series circuit it is the inverse, X/R.

questions.question: What is the resonant frequency of an RLC circuit if R is 33 ohms, L is 50 microhenries, and C is 10 picofarads?
What is the half-power bandwidth of a resonant circuit that has a resonant frequency of 7.1 MHz and a Q of 150?
What is the half-power bandwidth of a resonant circuit that has a resonant frequency of 3.7 MHz and a Q of 118?
What is an effect of increasing Q in a series resonant circuit?
answers: Fewer components are needed for the same performance
questions.explanation: The voltage across L and across C at series resonance is Q times the applied voltage. Higher Q means higher internal voltages, which matters for component ratings in tuners.

questions.question: What is the term for the time required for the capacitor in an RC circuit to be charged to 63.2% of the applied voltage or to discharge to 36.8% of its initial voltage?
questions.explanation: One time constant (τ = RC) is the time to charge to 63.2% (1 − e⁻¹) or discharge to 36.8% (e⁻¹).

questions.question: What letter is commonly used to represent susceptance?
questions.explanation: Susceptance is B. Admittance is Y = G + jB, where G is conductance.

questions.question: How is impedance in polar form converted to an equivalent admittance?
answers: Take the reciprocal of the angle and change the sign of the magnitude
Take the reciprocal of the magnitude and change the sign of the angle
Take the square root of the magnitude and add 180 degrees to the angle
Square the magnitude and subtract 90 degrees from the angle
questions.explanation: Y = 1/Z. In polar form that is 1/|Z| at an angle of −θ: take the reciprocal of the magnitude and flip the sign of the angle.

questions.question: What is the time constant of a circuit having two 220-microfarad capacitors and two 1-megohm resistors, all in parallel?
questions.explanation: Two 1 MΩ resistors in parallel make 0.5 MΩ, and two 220 µF capacitors in parallel make 440 µF. τ = 0.5×10⁶ × 440×10⁻⁶ = 220 s.

questions.question: What is the effect on the magnitude of pure reactance when it is converted to susceptance?
answers: It is replaced by its reciprocal
questions.explanation: Susceptance B = 1/X, so the magnitude is replaced by its reciprocal. The sign convention also flips.

questions.question: What is susceptance?
answers: The magnetic impedance of a circuit
The ratio of magnetic field to electric field
A measure of the efficiency of a transformer
questions.explanation: Admittance Y = G + jB. Susceptance B is its imaginary part.

questions.question: What is the phase angle between the voltage across and the current through a series RLC circuit if XC is 500 ohms, R is 1 kilohm, and XL is 250 ohms?
answers: 68.2 degrees with the voltage leading the current
14.0 degrees with the voltage leading the current
14.0 degrees with the voltage lagging the current
68.2 degrees with the voltage lagging the current
questions.explanation: Net X = XL − XC = 250 − 500 = −250 Ω (capacitive). θ = arctan(250/1000) ≈ 14.0°. A capacitive circuit has the voltage lagging the current.

questions.question: What is the phase angle between the voltage across and the current through a series RLC circuit if XC is 300 ohms, R is 100 ohms, and XL is 100 ohms?
answers: 63 degrees with the voltage lagging the current
63 degrees with the voltage leading the current
27 degrees with the voltage leading the current
27 degrees with the voltage lagging the current
questions.explanation: Net X = 100 − 300 = −200 Ω (capacitive). θ = arctan(200/100) ≈ 63.4°, with the voltage lagging the current.

questions.question: What is the relationship between the AC current through a capacitor and the voltage across a capacitor?
answers: Voltage and current are in phase
Voltage and current are 180 degrees out of phase
questions.explanation: In a capacitor, current leads voltage by 90°, because i = C dv/dt. Mnemonic: ELI the ICE man, where in C, I comes before E.

questions.question: What is the relationship between the AC current through an inductor and the voltage across an inductor?
answers: Voltage and current are 180 degrees out of phase
Voltage and current are in phase
questions.explanation: In an inductor, voltage leads current by 90°, because v = L di/dt (ELI).

questions.question: What is the phase angle between the voltage across and the current through a series RLC circuit if XC is 25 ohms, R is 100 ohms, and XL is 75 ohms?
answers: 27 degrees with the voltage lagging the current
27 degrees with the voltage leading the current
63 degrees with the voltage lagging the current
63 degrees with the voltage leading the current
questions.explanation: Net X = 75 − 25 = +50 Ω (inductive). θ = arctan(50/100) ≈ 26.6° ≈ 27°, with the voltage leading the current.

questions.question: What is admittance?
answers: The term for the gain of a field effect transistor
The term for the on-impedance of a field effect transistor
questions.explanation: Admittance Y = 1/Z, the reciprocal of impedance, measured in siemens.

questions.question: Which of the following represents pure capacitive reactance of 100 ohms in rectangular notation?
questions.explanation: Rectangular form is R + jX. A pure capacitive reactance has R = 0 and a negative X, so it is 0 − j100.

questions.question: How are impedances described in polar coordinates?
questions.explanation: Polar form gives the magnitude |Z| and the phase angle θ.

questions.question: Which of the following represents a pure inductive reactance in polar coordinates?
questions.explanation: A pure inductance has Z = XL at an angle of +90°.

questions.question: What type of Y-axis scale is most often used for graphs of circuit frequency response?
questions.explanation: Frequency-response plots usually use a logarithmic (dB) amplitude axis so they can show a wide dynamic range.

questions.question: What kind of diagram is used to show the phase relationship between impedances at a given frequency?
questions.explanation: A phasor diagram shows magnitudes and phase angles as vectors at a given frequency.

questions.question: What does the impedance 50 - j25 ohms represent?
answers: 50 ohms resistance in series with 25 ohms inductive reactance
50 ohms resistance in series with 25 ohms capacitive reactance
25 ohms resistance in series with 50 ohms inductive reactance
25 ohms resistance in series with 50 ohms capacitive reactance
questions.explanation: In 50 − j25, the real part is 50 Ω of resistance and the −j part is 25 Ω of capacitive reactance in series.

questions.question: Where is the impedance of a pure resistance plotted on rectangular coordinates?
answers: On a line through the origin, slanted at 45 degrees
On a horizontal line, offset vertically above the horizontal axis
questions.explanation: A pure resistance has no reactive (j) part, so it sits on the horizontal (real) axis.

questions.question: What coordinate system is often used to display the phase angle of a circuit containing resistance, inductive, and/or capacitive reactance?
questions.explanation: Polar coordinates show magnitude and phase angle directly.

questions.question: When using rectangular coordinates to graph the impedance of a circuit, what do the axes represent?
answers: The X axis represents the resistive component, and the Y axis represents the reactive component
The X axis represents the reactive component, and the Y axis represents the resistive component
The X axis represents the phase angle, and the Y axis represents the magnitude
The X axis represents the magnitude, and the Y axis represents the phase angle
questions.explanation: On an impedance plot, the X (horizontal) axis is resistance R and the Y (vertical) axis is reactance: +j inductive, −j capacitive.

questions.question: Which point on Figure E5-1 best represents the impedance of a series circuit consisting of a 400-ohm resistor and a 38-picofarad capacitor at 14 MHz?
Which point in Figure E5-1 best represents the impedance of a series circuit consisting of a 300-ohm resistor and an 18-microhenry inductor at 3.505 MHz?
Which point on Figure E5-1 best represents the impedance of a series circuit consisting of a 300-ohm resistor and a 19-picofarad capacitor at 21.200 MHz?
What is the result of conductor skin effect?
answers: Resistance increases as frequency increases because RF current flows closer to the surface
Resistance decreases as frequency increases because electron mobility increases
Resistance increases as temperature increases because of the change in thermal coefficient
Resistance decreases as temperature increases because of the change in thermal coefficient
questions.explanation: At RF, current crowds toward the conductor surface (skin depth ∝ 1/√f). The effective cross-section shrinks, so resistance rises with frequency.

questions.question: Why is it important to keep lead lengths short for components used in circuits for VHF and above?
answers: To increase the thermal time constant
questions.explanation: Every lead has inductance, about 1 nH per mm. At VHF and up, XL = 2πfL of even short leads becomes significant, so keep them short.

questions.question: What is the phase relationship between current and voltage for reactive power?
answers: They are 90 degrees out of phase
They are 45 degrees out of phase
questions.explanation: Reactive power is the product of voltage and current that are 90° out of phase. Its average real power is zero.

questions.question: Why are short connections used at microwave frequencies?
answers: To reduce phase shift along the connection
questions.explanation: At microwave frequencies even a few millimetres of connection is a sizable fraction of a wavelength and adds phase shift. Short connections minimize it.

questions.question: What parasitic characteristic causes electrolytic capacitors to be unsuitable for use at RF?
questions.explanation: Electrolytic capacitors have large parasitic inductance (ESL) from their rolled-foil construction, so they act like inductors at RF.

questions.question: What parasitic characteristic creates an inductor’s self-resonance?
questions.explanation: Capacitance between turns, in parallel with the coil's inductance, forms a parallel resonant circuit at the self-resonant frequency.

questions.question: What combines to create the self-resonance of a component?
answers: The component’s nominal and parasitic reactance
The component’s electrical length and impedance
questions.explanation: Self-resonance happens where the component's intended reactance cancels its parasitic reactance (for example a capacitor's C and its lead inductance).

questions.question: What is the primary cause of loss in film capacitors at RF?
questions.explanation: The pool attributes RF loss in film capacitors mainly to skin effect in the thin metallized electrodes and leads.
questions.explanationNote: Pool attributes film capacitor RF loss to skin effect; many references also cite dielectric loss. Explanation follows the key.

questions.question: What happens to reactive power in ideal inductors and capacitors?
answers: It is dissipated as heat in the circuit
Energy is stored in magnetic or electric fields, but power is not dissipated
It is canceled by Coulomb forces in the capacitor and inductor
It is dissipated in the formation of inductive and capacitive fields
questions.explanation: Ideal L and C store energy in magnetic and electric fields and give it back each cycle. No power is dissipated.

questions.question: As a conductor’s diameter increases, what is the effect on its electrical length?
answers: Thickness has no effect on electrical length
questions.explanation: A thicker conductor has more end capacitance and a lower velocity factor, so it is electrically longer. That is why fat dipoles are cut shorter.

questions.question: How much real power is consumed in a circuit consisting of a 100-ohm resistor in series with a 100-ohm inductive reactance drawing 1 ampere?
questions.explanation: Only the resistor dissipates real power: P = I²R = 1² × 100 = 100 W. The reactance dissipates none.

questions.question: What is reactive power?
answers: Power consumed by an inductor’s wire resistance
The power consumed in inductors and capacitors
questions.explanation: Reactive power (VAR) circulates between the source and the reactances without doing work. It is wattless power.

questions.question: In what application is gallium arsenide used as a semiconductor material?
questions.explanation: GaAs has much higher electron mobility than silicon, so GaAs devices (MESFETs, pHEMTs) are fast and low-noise at microwave frequencies.

questions.question: Which of the following semiconductor materials contains excess free electrons?
questions.explanation: N-type material is doped with donor atoms such as phosphorus or arsenic, which contribute excess free electrons.

questions.question: Why does a PN-junction diode not conduct current when reverse biased?
answers: Only P-type semiconductor material can conduct current
Only N-type semiconductor material can conduct current
Holes in P-type material and electrons in the N-type material are separated by the applied voltage, widening the depletion region
Excess holes in P-type material combine with the electrons in N-type material, converting the entire diode into an insulator
questions.explanation: Reverse bias pulls holes and electrons away from the junction. The depletion region widens and contains no mobile carriers, so essentially no current flows apart from a tiny leakage current.

questions.question: What is the name given to an impurity atom that adds holes to a semiconductor crystal structure?
questions.explanation: Acceptor impurities (trivalent atoms such as boron) accept electrons and so create holes, making P-type material.

questions.question: How does DC input impedance at the gate of a field-effect transistor (FET) compare with that of a bipolar transistor?
answers: An FET has lower input impedance
An FET has higher input impedance
questions.explanation: A FET's gate is a reverse-biased junction (JFET) or insulated by oxide (MOSFET), so its DC input impedance is far higher than a BJT's forward-biased base-emitter junction.

questions.question: What is the beta of a bipolar junction transistor?
answers: The frequency at which the current gain is reduced to 0.707
The change in collector current with respect to the change in base current
The breakdown voltage of the base-to-collector junction
questions.explanation: Beta (hFE) is the common-emitter current gain: β = ΔIc/ΔIb.

questions.question: Which of the following indicates that a silicon NPN junction transistor is biased on?
answers: Base-to-emitter resistance of approximately 6 ohms to 7 ohms
Base-to-emitter resistance of approximately 0.6 ohms to 0.7 ohms
Base-to-emitter voltage of approximately 6 volts to 7 volts
Base-to-emitter voltage of approximately 0.6 volts to 0.7 volts
questions.explanation: A silicon base-emitter junction starts conducting at about 0.6–0.7 V. Seeing that VBE means the transistor is biased on.

questions.question: What is the term for the frequency at which the grounded-base current gain of a bipolar junction transistor has decreased to 0.7 of the gain obtainable at 1 kHz?
questions.explanation: The alpha cutoff frequency is where the common-base current gain (α) falls to 0.707 (−3 dB) of its low-frequency value.

questions.question: What is a depletion-mode field-effect transistor (FET)?
answers: An FET that exhibits a current flow between source and drain when no gate voltage is applied
An FET that has no current flow between source and drain when no gate voltage is applied
An FET that exhibits very high electron mobility due to a lack of holes in the N-type material
An FET for which holes are the majority carriers
questions.explanation: A depletion-mode FET conducts with zero gate voltage. A gate voltage must be applied to deplete the channel and turn it off.

questions.question: In Figure E6-1, which is the schematic symbol for an N-channel dual-gate MOSFET?
questions.explanation: In Figure E6-1, symbols 4 and 5 have two gates (G1 and G2), so they are dual-gate MOSFETs. Symbol 4 is the N-channel version (arrow pointing in toward the channel).
questions.explanationNote: Arrow-direction detail for symbol 4 described from convention; verify against figure.

questions.question: In Figure E6-1, which is the schematic symbol for a P-channel junction FET?
questions.explanation: Symbol 1 is a junction FET (the gate connects directly to the channel, with no insulating gap). Its gate arrow points away from the channel, which indicates P-channel.
questions.explanationNote: Visual identification of symbol 1 (P-channel JFET) relies on the pool key.

questions.question: What is the purpose of connecting Zener diodes between a MOSFET gate and its source or drain?
answers: To provide a voltage reference for the correct amount of reverse-bias gate voltage
To protect the substrate from excessive voltages
To keep the gate voltage within specifications and prevent the device from overheating
To protect the gate from static damage
questions.explanation: Back-to-back Zeners from gate to source clamp static or transient voltages that would otherwise puncture the thin gate oxide.

questions.question: What is the most useful characteristic of a Zener diode?
answers: A constant current drop under conditions of varying voltage
A constant voltage drop under conditions of varying current
An internal capacitance that varies with the applied voltage
questions.explanation: In reverse breakdown, a Zener holds an almost constant voltage over a wide range of current, which makes it a voltage reference or regulator.

questions.question: Which characteristic of a Schottky diode makes it a better choice than a silicon junction diode for use as a power supply rectifier?
questions.explanation: A Schottky (metal-semiconductor) diode drops about 0.2–0.4 V in the forward direction, compared with about 0.7 V for silicon PN. That means less loss and heat in a rectifier. It also switches quickly.

questions.question: What property of an LED's semiconductor material determines its forward voltage drop?
questions.explanation: An LED's forward voltage is set by its band gap. Wider band gaps give shorter-wavelength (bluer) light and a higher Vf.

questions.question: What type of semiconductor device is designed for use as a voltage-controlled capacitor?
questions.explanation: A varactor's depletion-region capacitance changes with reverse bias, so it is used as a voltage-controlled capacitor in VCOs and tuning circuits.

questions.question: What characteristic of a PIN diode makes it useful as an RF switch?
answers: Ability to dissipate large amounts of power
Reverse bias controls its forward voltage drop
questions.explanation: The PIN diode's wide intrinsic layer gives very low junction capacitance when reverse biased, so it blocks RF well when off. Forward bias makes it a low-resistance path.

questions.question: Which of the following is a common use of a Schottky diode?
answers: In oscillator circuits as the negative resistance element
As a variable capacitance in an automatic frequency control circuit
In power supplies as a constant voltage reference
As a VHF/UHF mixer or detector
questions.explanation: Schottky diodes have low capacitance and little charge storage, so they are fast. They make good VHF/UHF mixers and detectors.

questions.question: What causes a junction diode to fail from excessive current?
questions.explanation: Too much forward current overheats the junction, and the excessive junction temperature destroys the diode.

questions.question: Which of the following is a Schottky barrier diode?
questions.explanation: A Schottky barrier diode is formed by a metal-semiconductor junction.

questions.question: What is a common use for point-contact diodes?
questions.explanation: Point-contact diodes (such as the 1N34 germanium diode) have very low capacitance and are traditionally used as RF detectors.

questions.question: In Figure E6-2, which is the schematic symbol for a Schottky diode?
questions.explanation: In Figure E6-2, the Schottky diode symbol (6) has the cathode bar drawn with S-shaped hooks at its ends.

questions.question: What is used to control the attenuation of RF signals by a PIN diode?
answers: Reverse voltage larger than the RF signal
Capacitance of an RF coupling capacitor
questions.explanation: A PIN diode's RF resistance is set by its forward DC bias current. More current means lower RF resistance, so the bias current controls the attenuation.

questions.question: What is the function of hysteresis in a comparator?
answers: To prevent input noise from causing unstable output signals
To allow the comparator to be used with AC input signals
To cause the output to continually change states
questions.explanation: Hysteresis gives a comparator separate switching thresholds for rising and falling inputs, so noise near the threshold cannot make the output chatter.

questions.question: What happens when the level of a comparator’s input signal crosses the threshold voltage?
answers: The IC input can be damaged
The comparator changes its output state
The reference level appears at the output
questions.explanation: A comparator's output switches state when the input crosses the reference (threshold) voltage.

questions.question: What is tri-state logic?
answers: Logic devices with 0, 1, and high-impedance output states
Logic devices that utilize ternary math
Logic with three output impedances which can be selected to better match the load impedance
questions.explanation: Tri-state outputs can be 0, 1 or high-impedance (off). That lets several devices share a bus.

questions.question: Which of the following is an advantage of BiCMOS logic?
answers: Its simplicity results in much less expensive devices than standard CMOS
It is immune to electrostatic damage
It has the high input impedance of CMOS and the low output impedance of bipolar transistors
questions.explanation: BiCMOS combines a CMOS input (high input impedance, low power) with a bipolar output (low impedance, strong drive).

questions.question: Which of the following digital logic families has the lowest power consumption?
questions.explanation: Static CMOS draws current almost only while switching, so it uses the least power of these families.

questions.question: Why do CMOS digital integrated circuits have high immunity to noise on the input signal or power supply?
answers: The input switching threshold is about twice the power supply voltage
The input switching threshold is about half the power supply voltage
questions.explanation: The CMOS switching threshold is about half the supply voltage, so noise must swing roughly Vdd/2 to cause a false transition.

questions.question: What best describes a pull-up or pull-down resistor?
answers: A resistor in a keying circuit used to reduce key clicks
A resistor connected to the positive or negative supply used to establish a voltage when an input or output is an open circuit
A resistor that ensures that an oscillator frequency does not drift
A resistor connected to an op-amp output that prevents signals from exceeding the power supply voltage
questions.explanation: A pull-up or pull-down resistor ties a line to the positive supply or ground, giving it a defined logic level when nothing is driving it (open circuit or open collector).

questions.question: In Figure E6-3, which is the schematic symbol for a NAND gate?
questions.explanation: In Figure E6-3, symbol 2 is an AND shape with an inversion bubble on the output, which is NAND.

questions.question: What is used to design the configuration of a field-programmable gate array (FPGA)?
questions.explanation: FPGA logic is described in a hardware description language such as VHDL or Verilog, then synthesized into the device configuration.

questions.question: In Figure E6-3, which is the schematic symbol for a NOR gate?
questions.explanation: Symbol 4 is an OR shape with an output bubble, which is NOR.

questions.question: In Figure E6-3, which is the schematic symbol for the NOT operation (inversion)?
questions.explanation: Symbol 5 is a triangle buffer with an output bubble, an inverter (NOT).

questions.question: What is piezoelectricity?
answers: The ability of materials to generate electromagnetic waves of a certain frequency when voltage is applied
A characteristic of materials that have an index of refraction which depends on the polarization of the electromagnetic wave passing through it
A characteristic of materials that generate a voltage when stressed and that flex when a voltage is applied
The ability of materials to generate voltage when an electromagnetic wave of a certain frequency is applied
questions.explanation: Piezoelectric materials such as quartz produce a voltage when mechanically stressed, and deform when a voltage is applied.

questions.question: What is the equivalent circuit of a quartz crystal?
answers: Series RLC in parallel with a shunt C representing electrode and stray capacitance
Parallel RLC, where C is the parallel combination of resonance capacitance of the crystal and electrode and stray capacitance
Series RLC, where C is the parallel combination of resonance capacitance of the crystal and electrode and stray capacitance
Parallel RLC, where C is the series combination of resonance capacitance of the crystal and electrode and stray capacitance
questions.explanation: A crystal's motional arm (series R, L and C) is in parallel with the shunt capacitance C0 of the electrodes and holder. That is why a crystal has both series and parallel resonances.

questions.question: Which of the following is an aspect of the piezoelectric effect?
answers: Mechanical deformation of material due to the application of a voltage
Mechanical deformation of material due to the application of a magnetic field
Generation of electrical energy in the presence of light
Increased conductivity in the presence of light
questions.explanation: The converse piezoelectric effect is mechanical deformation when a voltage is applied.

questions.question: Why are cores of inductors and transformers sometimes constructed of thin layers?
answers: To reduce power loss from eddy currents in the core
To increase the cutoff frequency by reducing capacitance
To save cost by reducing the amount of magnetic material
questions.explanation: Laminations are insulated from each other, which breaks up the eddy-current paths in the core and reduces I²R heating.

questions.question: How do ferrite and powdered iron compare for use in an inductor core?
answers: Ferrite cores generally have lower initial permeability
Ferrite cores generally have better temperature stability
Ferrite cores generally require fewer turns to produce a given inductance value
Ferrite cores are easier to use with surface-mount technology
questions.explanation: Ferrite has much higher permeability than powdered iron. Since L ∝ μN², fewer turns are needed for the same inductance.

questions.question: What core material property determines the inductance of an inductor?
questions.explanation: Inductance is proportional to the core's permeability (μ), together with the number of turns and the geometry.

questions.question: Which of the following materials has the highest temperature stability of its magnetic characteristics?
questions.explanation: Powdered iron has better temperature stability than ferrite. Brass and aluminum are not magnetic.

questions.question: What devices are commonly used as VHF and UHF parasitic suppressors at the input and output terminals of a transistor HF amplifier?
questions.explanation: Ferrite beads on transistor leads add loss at VHF/UHF without affecting HF signals, which damps parasitic oscillations.

questions.question: What is a primary advantage of using a toroidal core instead of a solenoidal core in an inductor?
answers: Toroidal cores confine most of the magnetic field within the core material
Toroidal cores make it easier to couple the magnetic energy into other components
Toroidal cores have lower Q characteristics
questions.explanation: A toroid keeps nearly all of its flux inside the closed core, so it radiates and picks up very little and couples less to nearby parts.

questions.question: Which type of core material decreases inductance when inserted into a coil?
questions.explanation: Brass is non-magnetic and conductive. Eddy currents induced in a brass slug oppose the coil's field, which reduces inductance.

questions.question: What causes inductor saturation?
answers: Operation at too high a frequency
Selecting a core with low permeability
Selecting a core with excessive permittivity
questions.explanation: Saturation happens when the flux density exceeds what the core can support. Permeability then collapses and the inductance drops.

questions.question: Why is gallium arsenide (GaAs) useful for semiconductor devices operating at UHF and higher frequencies?
questions.explanation: GaAs's higher electron mobility gives faster transit times and lower noise at UHF and microwave frequencies.

questions.question: Which of the following device packages is a through-hole type?
questions.explanation: A DIP (dual in-line package) has pins that go through holes in the board. PLCC, BGA and SOT are surface-mount packages.

questions.question: Which of the following materials supports the highest frequency of operation when used in MMICs?
questions.explanation: Per the pool key, gallium nitride (GaN) supports the highest operating frequency among these MMIC materials, thanks to its high electron velocity and breakdown field.
questions.explanationNote: GaN as highest-frequency MMIC material follows the pool key.

questions.question: Which is the most common input and output impedance of MMICs?
questions.explanation: Most MMICs are designed with 50 Ω input and output so they drop straight into standard RF systems.

questions.question: Which of the following noise figure values is typical of a low-noise UHF preamplifier?
questions.explanation: Good UHF low-noise preamps achieve noise figures well under 1 dB, for example 0.5 dB. Noise figure can't be negative, and dBm is a power unit.

questions.question: What characteristics of MMICs make them a popular choice for VHF through microwave circuits?
answers: The ability to retrieve information from a single signal, even in the presence of other strong signals
Extremely high Q factor and high stability over a wide temperature range
Nearly infinite gain, very high input impedance, and very low output impedance
Controlled gain, low noise figure, and constant input and output impedance over the specified frequency range
questions.explanation: MMICs offer predictable gain, low noise and a steady 50 Ω match across a wide band, so they make simple gain blocks.

questions.question: What type of transmission line is often used for connections to MMICs?
questions.explanation: MMICs are mounted on PCBs with microstrip lines of controlled impedance, usually 50 Ω.

questions.question: How is power supplied to the most common type of MMIC?
answers: Through a capacitor and RF choke connected to the amplifier input lead
Through a resistor and/or RF choke connected to the amplifier output lead
Directly to the bias voltage (Vcc) lead
questions.explanation: A common MMIC gets its bias through its output pin, fed via a resistor and/or RF choke from the supply.

questions.question: Which of the following component package types have the least parasitic effects at frequencies above the HF range?
questions.explanation: Surface-mount parts have little or no lead length, so their parasitic inductance and capacitance are much lower above HF.

questions.question: What advantage does surface-mount technology offer at RF compared to using through-hole components?
answers: Components have less parasitic inductance and capacitance
questions.explanation: SMT means a smaller layout, shorter traces and lower parasitics. All the choices are correct.

questions.question: What is a characteristic of DIP packaging used for integrated circuits?
answers: Extremely low stray capacitance (dielectrically isolated package)
Extremely high resistance between pins (doubly insulated package)
Two chips in each package (dual in package)
Two rows of connecting pins on opposite sides of package (dual in-line package)
questions.explanation: DIP stands for dual in-line package: two parallel rows of pins on opposite sides.

questions.question: Why are DIP through-hole package ICs not typically used at UHF and higher frequencies?
answers: Epoxy coating is conductive above 300 MHz
Unsuitable for combining analog and digital signals
questions.explanation: DIP leads and their board traces are long enough to add significant inductance and capacitance at UHF.

questions.question: What absorbs the energy from light falling on a photovoltaic cell?
questions.explanation: Photon energy is absorbed by electrons in the semiconductor, freeing them to carry current.

questions.question: What happens to photoconductive material when light shines on it?
questions.explanation: Light creates extra charge carriers in a photoconductor, so its resistance drops.

questions.question: What is the most common configuration of an optoisolator or optocoupler?
questions.explanation: A typical optocoupler is an LED shining on a phototransistor inside a light-tight package.

questions.question: What is the photovoltaic effect?
answers: The conversion of voltage to current when exposed to light
The conversion of light to electrical energy
The effect that causes a photodiode to emit light when a voltage is applied
The effect that causes a phototransistor’s beta to decrease when exposed to light
questions.explanation: The photovoltaic effect converts light directly into electrical energy.

questions.question: Which of the following describes an optical shaft encoder?
answers: A device that detects rotation by interrupting a light source with a patterned wheel
A device that measures the strength of a beam of light using analog-to-digital conversion
An optical computing device in which light is coupled between devices by fiber optics
A device for generating RTTY signals by means of a rotating light source
questions.explanation: An optical shaft encoder senses rotation with a slotted or patterned wheel that interrupts a light beam, producing pulses.

questions.question: Which of these materials is most commonly used to create photoconductive devices?
questions.explanation: Photoconductive devices are usually made from crystalline semiconductors such as CdS or silicon.

questions.question: What is a solid-state relay?
answers: A relay that uses transistors to drive the relay coil
A device that uses semiconductors to implement the functions of an electromechanical relay
A mechanical relay that latches in the on or off state each time it is pulsed
A semiconductor switch that uses a monostable multivibrator circuit
questions.explanation: A solid-state relay uses semiconductors (an optocoupler plus a triac or MOSFET) to do a relay's switching job with no moving parts.

questions.question: Why are optoisolators often used in conjunction with solid-state circuits that control 120 VAC circuits?
answers: Optoisolators provide a low-impedance link between a control circuit and a power circuit
Optoisolators provide impedance matching between the control circuit and power circuit
Optoisolators provide an electrical isolation between a control circuit and the circuit being switched
Optoisolators eliminate the effects of reflected light in the control circuit
questions.explanation: An optoisolator couples the control signal only by light, giving galvanic isolation between low-voltage logic and the 120 VAC circuit.

questions.question: What is the efficiency of a photovoltaic cell?
answers: The output RF power divided by the input DC power
The output in lumens divided by the input power in watts
The open-circuit voltage divided by the short-circuit current under full illumination
The relative fraction of light that is converted to current
questions.explanation: PV efficiency is the fraction of incident light energy converted into electrical output.

questions.question: What is the most common material used in power-generating photovoltaic cells?
questions.explanation: Most power-generating solar cells are crystalline or polycrystalline silicon.

questions.question: What is the approximate open-circuit voltage produced by a fully illuminated silicon photovoltaic cell?
questions.explanation: A fully lit silicon PV cell produces about 0.5 V (≈0.5–0.6 V) open circuit, so panels connect many cells in series.

questions.question: Which circuit is bistable?
questions.explanation: A flip-flop has two stable states and stays in either one until it is triggered, so it is bistable.

questions.question: What is the function of a decade counter?
answers: It produces one output pulse for every 10 input pulses
It decodes a decimal number for display on a seven-segment LED display
It produces 10 output pulses for every input pulse
It decodes a binary number for display on a seven-segment LED display
questions.explanation: A decade counter counts 10 input pulses and then produces one output pulse (carry) and resets, dividing by 10.

questions.question: Which of the following can divide the frequency of a pulse train by 2?
questions.explanation: A toggle (T or J-K) flip-flop changes state on each clock edge, so its output runs at half the input frequency.

questions.question: How many flip-flops are required to divide a signal frequency by 16?
questions.explanation: Each flip-flop divides by 2, and 2⁴ = 16, so 4 flip-flops are needed.

questions.question: Which of the following circuits continuously alternates between two states without an external clock signal?
questions.explanation: An astable multivibrator has no stable state. It free-runs, flipping between two states to make a square wave.

questions.question: What is a characteristic of a monostable multivibrator?
answers: It switches temporarily to an alternate state for a set time
It produces a continuous square wave
It stores one bit of data
It maintains a constant output voltage, regardless of variations in the input voltage
questions.explanation: A monostable (one-shot) multivibrator flips to its unstable state when triggered and returns after a time set by an RC network.

questions.question: What logical operation does a NAND gate perform?
answers: It produces a 0 at its output only if all inputs are 0
It produces a 1 at its output only if all inputs are 1
It produces a 0 at its output if some but not all inputs are 1
It produces a 0 at its output only if all inputs are 1
questions.explanation: NAND is AND followed by NOT. The output is 0 only when all inputs are 1.

questions.question: What logical operation does an OR gate perform?
answers: It produces a 1 at its output if any input is 1
It produces a 0 at its output if all inputs are 1
It produces a 0 at its output if some but not all inputs are 1
It produces a 1 at its output if all inputs are 0
questions.explanation: OR outputs 1 if any input is 1, and 0 only if all inputs are 0.

questions.question: What logical operation is performed by a two-input exclusive NOR gate?
answers: It produces a 0 at its output only if all inputs are 0
It produces a 1 at its output only if all inputs are 1
It produces a 0 at its output if one and only one of its inputs is 1
It produces a 1 at its output if one and only one input is 1
questions.explanation: XNOR is the complement of XOR. The output is 1 when the inputs are equal and 0 when exactly one input is 1.

questions.question: What is a truth table?
answers: A list of inputs and corresponding outputs for an op-amp
A list of inputs and corresponding outputs for a digital device
A diagram showing logic states when the digital gate output is true
A table of logic symbols that indicate the logic states of an op-amp
questions.explanation: A truth table lists every input combination for a digital device and the output it produces.

questions.question: What does “positive logic” mean in reference to logic devices?
answers: The logic devices have high noise immunity
High voltage represents a 1, low voltage a 0
The logic circuit is in the “true” condition
1s and 0s are defined as different positive voltage levels
questions.explanation: In positive logic, the higher voltage is logic 1 and the lower voltage is logic 0.

questions.question: For what portion of the signal cycle does each active element in a push-pull, Class AB amplifier conduct?
answers: More than 180 degrees but less than 360 degrees
questions.explanation: Class AB biases each device slightly on, so it conducts for more than half the cycle (over 180°) but less than the full 360°. This reduces crossover distortion compared with Class B.

questions.question: What is a Class D amplifier?
answers: An amplifier that uses switching technology to achieve high efficiency
A low power amplifier that uses a differential amplifier for improved linearity
An amplifier that uses drift-mode FETs for high efficiency
An amplifier biased to be relatively free from distortion
questions.explanation: A Class D amplifier switches its devices fully on or off (PWM or other switching), so efficiency is very high, often above 90%.

questions.question: What circuit is required at the output of an RF switching amplifier?
answers: A filter to remove harmonic content
A high-pass filter to compensate for low gain at low frequencies
A matched load resistor to prevent damage by switching transients
A temperature compensating load resistor to improve linearity
questions.explanation: A switching amplifier's output is rich in harmonics, so a low-pass or band-pass filter is needed to remove them before the antenna.

questions.question: What is the operating point of a Class A common emitter amplifier?
answers: Approximately halfway between saturation and cutoff
Approximately halfway between the emitter voltage and the base voltage
At a point where the bias resistor equals the load resistor
At a point where the load line intersects the zero bias current curve
questions.explanation: A Class A amplifier is biased midway between cutoff and saturation, so the whole signal swing stays in the linear region.

questions.question: What can be done to prevent unwanted oscillations in an RF power amplifier?
answers: Tune the stage for minimum loading
Tune both the input and output for maximum power
Install parasitic suppressors and/or neutralize the stage
Use a phase inverter in the output filter
questions.explanation: Parasitic suppressors damp VHF parasitics, and neutralization cancels the feedback through the device's internal capacitance. Both prevent self-oscillation.

questions.question: What is a characteristic of a grounded-grid amplifier?
questions.explanation: In a grounded-grid amplifier the drive goes into the cathode, which gives a low input impedance, around 50–100 Ω for many tubes. That makes it easy to drive directly from a transceiver.

questions.question: Which of the following is the likely result of using a Class C amplifier to amplify a single-sideband phone signal?
questions.explanation: Class C is highly nonlinear. It distorts SSB's varying-amplitude envelope, producing splatter and excessive bandwidth.

questions.question: Why are switching amplifiers more efficient than linear amplifiers?
answers: Switching amplifiers operate at higher voltages
The switching device is at saturation or cutoff most of the time
Linear amplifiers have high gain resulting in higher harmonic content
questions.explanation: When fully on, a switch has nearly zero voltage across it, and when off it carries almost no current. Either way P = V × I is small, so little power is lost.

questions.question: What is characteristic of an emitter follower (or common collector) amplifier?
answers: Low input impedance and phase inversion from input to output
Acts as an OR circuit if one input is grounded
questions.explanation: An emitter follower has a voltage gain of about 1, no phase inversion (output in phase with input), high input impedance and low output impedance.

questions.question: In Figure E7-1, what is the purpose of R1 and R2?
questions.explanation: In Figure E7-1, R1 and R2 form a voltage divider from the supply that sets the base bias voltage.

questions.question: In Figure E7-1, what is the purpose of R3?
questions.explanation: R3, the emitter resistor, gives self-bias and stabilization through negative feedback. If emitter current rises, the emitter voltage rises and VBE falls.
questions.explanationNote: Pool calls R3 'self bias'; explanation describes emitter degeneration.

questions.question: What type of amplifier circuit is shown in Figure E7-1?
questions.explanation: In Figure E7-1 the input goes to the base and the output is taken from the collector. The emitter is common (it goes to ground through R3 and is bypassed by C3), so this is a common-emitter amplifier.

questions.question: How are the capacitors and inductors of a low-pass filter Pi-network arranged between the network’s input and output?
answers: Two inductors are in series between the input and output, and a capacitor is connected between the two inductors and ground
Two capacitors are in series between the input and output, and an inductor is connected between the two capacitors and ground
An inductor is connected between the input and ground, another inductor is connected between the output and ground, and a capacitor is connected between the input and output
A capacitor is connected between the input and ground, another capacitor is connected between the output and ground, and an inductor is connected between the input and output
questions.explanation: A low-pass pi network has shunt capacitors at the input and output with a series inductor between them, which passes low frequencies and shunts high ones to ground.

questions.question: What is the frequency response of a T-network with series capacitors and a shunt inductor?
questions.explanation: Series capacitors pass high frequencies, and a shunt inductor sends low frequencies to ground, so the network is high-pass.

questions.question: What is the purpose of adding an inductor to a Pi-network to create a Pi-L-network?
questions.explanation: Adding an output series inductor to a pi network (Pi-L) adds another low-pass section, which improves harmonic suppression.

questions.question: How does an impedance-matching circuit transform a complex impedance to a resistive impedance?
answers: It introduces negative resistance to cancel the resistive part of impedance
It introduces transconductance to cancel the reactive part of impedance
It cancels the reactive part of the impedance and changes the resistive part to the desired value
Reactive currents are dissipated in matched resistances
questions.explanation: A matching network adds equal and opposite reactance to cancel the load's reactive part, and transforms the resistive part to the desired value (for example 50 Ω).

questions.question: Which filter type has ripple in the passband and a sharp cutoff?
questions.explanation: A Chebyshev filter accepts ripple in the passband in exchange for a steeper transition than a Butterworth filter.

questions.question: What are the characteristics of an elliptical filter?
answers: Gradual passband rolloff with minimal stop-band ripple
Extremely flat response over its pass band with gradually rounded stop-band corners
Extremely sharp cutoff with one or more notches in the stop band
Gradual passband rolloff with extreme stop-band ripple
questions.explanation: Elliptic (Cauer) filters place zeros (notches) in the stopband, giving the sharpest cutoff, with ripple in both the passband and the stopband.

questions.question: Which describes a Pi-L network?
answers: A Pi-network with an additional output series inductor
A network with only three discrete parts
A matching network in which all components are isolated from ground
questions.explanation: A Pi-L network is a pi network followed by a series inductor at the output.

questions.question: Which of the following is most frequently used as a band-pass or notch filter in VHF and UHF transceivers?
questions.explanation: Helical resonator filters are compact, high-Q band-pass and notch filters widely used in VHF/UHF radios.

questions.question: What is a crystal lattice filter?
answers: A power supply filter made with interlaced quartz crystals
An audio filter made with four quartz crystals that resonate at 1 kHz intervals
A filter using lattice-shaped quartz crystals for high-Q performance
A filter for low-level signals made using quartz crystals
questions.explanation: A crystal lattice filter uses several quartz crystals for a narrow, steep-sided passband. It is used as an IF filter for low-level signals.

questions.question: Which of the following filters is used in a 2-meter band repeater duplexer?
questions.explanation: Repeater duplexers use high-Q cavity resonators to separate the transmit and receive frequencies, which are only 600 kHz apart on 2 m.

questions.question: Which of the following measures a filter’s ability to reject signals in adjacent channels?
questions.explanation: Shape factor is the ratio of the bandwidth at high attenuation (for example −60 dB) to the bandwidth at −6 dB. A lower value means steeper skirts and better adjacent-channel rejection.

questions.question: How does a linear electronic voltage regulator work?
answers: It has a ramp voltage as its output
It eliminates the need for a pass transistor
The control element duty cycle is proportional to the line or load conditions
The conduction of a control element is varied to maintain a constant output voltage
questions.explanation: A linear regulator continuously varies how hard its pass element conducts, so it drops whatever voltage is needed to hold the output constant.

questions.question: How does a switchmode voltage regulator work?
answers: By alternating the output between positive and negative voltages
By varying the duty cycle of pulses input to a filter
By varying the conductivity of a pass element
By switching between two Zener diode reference voltages
questions.explanation: A switching regulator varies the duty cycle of pulses fed into an LC filter. The average output voltage is set by the duty cycle.

questions.question: What device is used as a stable voltage reference?
questions.explanation: A Zener diode in reverse breakdown holds a stable voltage and serves as a reference.

questions.question: Which of the following describes a three-terminal voltage regulator?
questions.explanation: Three-terminal regulators such as the 78xx and LM317 are series regulators: a pass transistor sits in series with the load.

questions.question: Which of the following types of linear voltage regulator operates by loading the unregulated voltage source?
questions.explanation: A shunt regulator sits across the output and draws more or less current to load the source, which holds the voltage constant.

questions.question: What is the purpose of Q1 in the circuit shown in Figure E7-2?
answers: It provides negative feedback to improve regulation
It provides a constant load for the voltage source
It controls the current to keep the output voltage constant
It provides regulation by switching or “chopping” the input DC voltage
questions.explanation: In Figure E7-2, Q1 is the series pass transistor. Its base is held at the Zener voltage, so it adjusts its conduction to keep the output at about Vz − 0.7 V.

questions.question: What is the purpose of C2 in the circuit shown in Figure E7-2?
answers: It bypasses rectifier output ripple around D1
It is a brute force filter for the output
To provide fixed DC bias for Q1
questions.explanation: C2 is across Zener D1. It bypasses ripple and noise around the Zener, keeping the base reference clean.

questions.question: What type of circuit is shown in Figure E7-2?
questions.explanation: Figure E7-2 is a Zener-referenced series pass transistor regulator, which is a linear regulator.

questions.question: How is battery operating time calculated?
answers: Average current divided by capacity in amp-hours
Average current divided by internal resistance
Capacity in amp-hours divided by average current
Internal resistance divided by average current
questions.explanation: Operating time (hours) = capacity (Ah) ÷ average current (A). For example, 20 Ah at 4 A gives 5 h.

questions.question: Why is a switching type power supply less expensive and lighter than an equivalent linear power supply?
answers: The inverter design does not require an output filter circuit
The control circuitry uses less current, therefore smaller heat sinks are required
The high frequency inverter design uses much smaller transformers and filter components for an equivalent power output
It recovers power from the unused portion of the AC cycle, thus using fewer components
questions.explanation: Switchers convert at tens or hundreds of kHz, and transformer and filter size shrink as frequency rises. That makes the magnetics and capacitors much smaller, lighter and cheaper.

questions.question: What is the purpose of an inverter connected to a solar panel output?
answers: Reduce AC ripple on the output
Maintain voltage with varying illumination levels
Prevent discharge when panel is not illuminated
Convert the panel’s output from DC to AC
questions.explanation: A solar panel produces DC. An inverter converts it to AC for AC loads or the grid.

questions.question: What is the dropout voltage of a linear voltage regulator?
answers: Minimum input voltage for rated power dissipation
Maximum output voltage drop when the input voltage is varied over its specified range
Minimum input-to-output voltage required to maintain regulation
Maximum that the output voltage may decrease at rated load
questions.explanation: Dropout voltage is the minimum input-to-output difference a linear regulator needs in order to keep regulating.

questions.question: Which of the following calculates power dissipated by a series linear voltage regulator?
answers: Input voltage multiplied by input current
Input voltage divided by output current
Voltage difference from input to output multiplied by output current
Output voltage multiplied by output current
questions.explanation: The pass element drops (Vin − Vout) while carrying the load current, so P = (Vin − Vout) × Iout.

questions.question: What is the purpose of connecting equal-value resistors across power supply filter capacitors connected in series?
answers: Equalize the voltage across each capacitor
Discharge the capacitors when voltage is removed
Provide a minimum load on the supply
questions.explanation: Equalizing resistors balance the voltage across series capacitors, bleed them down after power-off, and provide a minimum load. All the choices are correct.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a step-start circuit in a high-voltage power supply?
answers: To provide a dual-voltage output for reduced power applications
To compensate for variations of the incoming line voltage
To prevent arcing across the input power switch or relay contacts
To allow the filter capacitors to charge gradually
questions.explanation: A step-start circuit limits the inrush current at turn-on (with a series resistor that is later shorted out), so the filter capacitors charge gradually.

questions.question: Which of the following can be used to generate FM phone signals?
answers: Balanced modulation of the audio amplifier
Reactance modulation of a local oscillator
Reactance modulation of the final amplifier
Balanced modulation of a local oscillator
questions.explanation: FM can be produced by applying audio to a reactance modulator on the oscillator, which varies its frequency.

questions.question: What is the function of a reactance modulator?
answers: Produce PM or FM signals by varying a resistance
Produce AM signals by varying an inductance
Produce AM signals by varying a resistance
Produce PM or FM signals by varying a capacitance
questions.explanation: A reactance modulator uses a variable reactance, typically a varactor's capacitance, to shift the oscillator's frequency or phase.

questions.question: What is a frequency discriminator?
answers: A circuit for filtering closely adjacent signals
A circuit for detecting FM signals
questions.explanation: A frequency discriminator converts frequency deviation into an amplitude (audio) output. It is an FM detector.

questions.question: What is one way to produce a single-sideband phone signal?
answers: Use a balanced modulator followed by a filter
Use a reactance modulator followed by a mixer
Use a loop modulator followed by a mixer
Use a product detector with a DSB signal
questions.explanation: A balanced modulator produces DSB with the carrier suppressed. A sideband filter then removes the unwanted sideband.

questions.question: What is added to an FM speech channel to boost the higher audio frequencies?
questions.explanation: Pre-emphasis boosts the higher audio frequencies before FM modulation to improve SNR. The receiver's de-emphasis undoes it.

questions.question: Why is de-emphasis used in FM communications receivers?
answers: For compatibility with transmitters using phase modulation
questions.explanation: Phase modulation inherently emphasizes higher audio frequencies, and FM transmitters add pre-emphasis to match. Receiver de-emphasis restores a flat response from such transmitters.
questions.explanationNote: Explanation follows pool key wording; de-emphasis primarily complements transmitter pre-emphasis.

questions.question: What is meant by the term “baseband” in radio communications?
answers: The lowest frequency band that the transmitter or receiver covers
The frequency range occupied by a message signal prior to modulation
The unmodulated bandwidth of the transmitted signal
The basic oscillator frequency in an FM transmitter that is multiplied to increase the deviation and carrier frequency
questions.explanation: Baseband is the frequency range of the original message (such as audio) before it modulates a carrier.

questions.question: What are the principal frequencies that appear at the output of a mixer?
answers: Two and four times the input frequency
The square root of the product of input frequencies
The two input frequencies along with their sum and difference frequencies
questions.explanation: An ideal mixer outputs f1 + f2 and |f1 − f2|. Real mixers also pass the original input frequencies.

questions.question: What occurs when the input signal levels to a mixer are too high?
answers: Excessive AGC voltage levels are generated
questions.explanation: Overdriving a mixer pushes it into strongly nonlinear operation, generating spurious higher-order mixing products.

questions.question: How does a diode envelope detector function?
answers: By rectification and filtering of RF signals
By breakdown of the Zener voltage
By mixing signals with noise in the transition region of the diode
By sensing the change of reactance in the diode with respect to frequency
questions.explanation: An envelope detector rectifies the RF with a diode and filters it with an RC network, recovering the AM envelope.

questions.question: Which type of detector is used for demodulating SSB signals?
questions.explanation: A product detector mixes SSB with a locally generated BFO or carrier to recover the audio.

questions.question: What is meant by “direct sampling” in software defined radios?
answers: Software is converted from source code to object code during operation of the receiver
I and Q signals are generated by digital processing without the use of RF amplification
Incoming RF is digitized by an analog-to-digital converter without being mixed with a local oscillator signal
A switching mixer is used to generate I and Q signals directly from the RF input
questions.explanation: A direct-sampling SDR feeds the RF, after filtering and possibly amplification, straight into a fast ADC. There is no analog mixing with a local oscillator. Tuning and demodulation are done digitally.
