questions.question: What kind of digital signal processing audio filter is used to remove unwanted noise from a received SSB signal?
questions.explanation: An adaptive filter continuously adjusts its coefficients to separate the correlated speech from uncorrelated noise. This is how DSP noise reduction works.

questions.question: What type of digital signal processing filter is used to generate an SSB signal?
questions.explanation: A Hilbert transform filter shifts all frequencies by 90°, producing the quadrature (Q) signal used in the phasing method of SSB generation.

questions.question: Which method generates an SSB signal using digital signal processing?
answers: Mixing products are converted to voltages and subtracted by adder circuits
A frequency synthesizer removes unwanted sidebands
Varying quartz crystal characteristics are emulated in digital form
Signals are combined in quadrature phase relationship
questions.explanation: DSP SSB uses the phasing method. I and Q versions of the audio and the carrier are combined in quadrature so that one sideband cancels.

questions.question: How frequently must an analog signal be sampled to be accurately reproduced?
answers: At least half the rate of the highest frequency component of the signal
At least twice the rate of the highest frequency component of the signal
At the same rate as the highest frequency component of the signal
At four times the rate of the highest frequency component of the signal
questions.explanation: By the Nyquist theorem, the sample rate must be at least twice the highest frequency in the signal.

questions.question: What is the minimum number of bits required to sample a signal with a range of 1 volt at a resolution of 1 millivolt?
questions.explanation: 1 V / 1 mV = 1000 levels. 2⁹ = 512 is too few and 2¹⁰ = 1024 is enough, so 10 bits are needed.

questions.question: What function is performed by a Fast Fourier Transform?
answers: Converting analog signals to digital form
Converting digital signals to analog form
Converting signals from the time domain to the frequency domain
Converting signals from the frequency domain to the time domain
questions.explanation: The FFT is an efficient algorithm for the discrete Fourier transform. It converts time-domain samples into frequency-domain (spectrum) data.

questions.question: What is the function of decimation?
answers: Converting data to binary-coded decimal form
Reducing the effective sample rate by removing samples
questions.explanation: Decimation lowers the sample rate by keeping only every Nth sample, after filtering.

questions.question: Why is an anti-aliasing filter required in a decimator?
answers: It removes high-frequency signal components that would otherwise be reproduced as lower frequency components
It peaks the response of the decimator, improving bandwidth
It removes low-frequency signal components to eliminate the need for DC restoration
It notches out the sampling frequency to avoid sampling errors
questions.explanation: After decimation the Nyquist frequency is lower. Content above the new limit would alias down to false low frequencies, so it must be filtered out first.

questions.question: What aspect of receiver analog-to-digital conversion determines the maximum receive bandwidth of a direct-sampling software defined radio (SDR)?
questions.explanation: Nyquist limits the usable bandwidth to half the sample rate. For example, a 122.88 MS/s ADC covers about 61 MHz.

questions.question: What sets the minimum detectable signal level for a direct-sampling software defined receiver in the absence of atmospheric or thermal noise?
answers: Reference voltage level and sample width in bits
questions.explanation: The smallest step an ADC can resolve, one LSB = Vref / 2^bits, sets the minimum detectable signal when no other noise is present.

questions.question: Which of the following is generally true of Finite Impulse Response (FIR) filters?
answers: FIR filters can delay all frequency components of the signal by the same amount
FIR filters are easier to implement for a given set of passband rolloff requirements
FIR filters can respond faster to impulses
questions.explanation: Symmetric FIR filters can have linear phase, which means a constant group delay: every frequency component is delayed by the same amount.

questions.question: What is the function of taps in a digital signal processing filter?
answers: To reduce excess signal pressure levels
Select the point at which baseband signals are generated
Provide incremental signal delays for filter algorithms
questions.explanation: Taps are the delayed sample points in the filter's delay line. Each one is multiplied by a coefficient and summed.

questions.question: Which of the following would allow a digital signal processing filter to create a sharper filter response?
questions.explanation: More taps give a longer impulse response, which allows a sharper (steeper) frequency response.

questions.question: What is the typical output impedance of an op-amp?
questions.explanation: An op-amp's output stage has a very low output impedance, ideally zero.

questions.question: What is the frequency response of the circuit in E7-3 if a capacitor is added across the feedback resistor?
questions.explanation: A capacitor across RF lowers the feedback impedance as frequency rises, so the gain falls at high frequencies: a low-pass response.

questions.question: What is the typical input impedance of an op-amp?
questions.explanation: Op-amp inputs (especially FET inputs) have a very high impedance, ideally infinite.

questions.question: What is meant by the term “op-amp input offset voltage”?
answers: The output voltage of the op-amp minus its input voltage
The difference between the output voltage of the op-amp and the input voltage required in the immediately following stage
The differential input voltage needed to bring the open loop output voltage to zero
The potential between the amplifier input terminals of the op-amp in an open loop condition
questions.explanation: Input offset voltage is the small differential input voltage needed to bring the open-loop output to zero. It comes from mismatches inside the op-amp.

questions.question: How can unwanted ringing and audio instability be prevented in an op-amp audio filter?
questions.explanation: High gain and high Q make active filters ring and tend to oscillate. Keeping both moderate keeps the filter stable.

questions.question: What is the gain-bandwidth of an operational amplifier?
answers: The maximum frequency for a filter circuit using that type of amplifier
The frequency at which the open-loop gain of the amplifier equals one
The gain of the amplifier at a filter’s cutoff frequency
The frequency at which the amplifier’s offset voltage is zero
questions.explanation: Gain-bandwidth is the frequency at which the open-loop gain falls to 1 (unity). For a single-pole op-amp, gain × bandwidth is constant.

questions.question: What voltage gain can be expected from the circuit in Figure E73 when R1 is 10 ohms and RF is 470 ohms?
questions.explanation: For an inverting amplifier, |Av| = RF/R1 = 470/10 = 47.

questions.question: How does the gain of an ideal operational amplifier vary with frequency?
answers: It increases linearly with increasing frequency
It decreases linearly with increasing frequency
It decreases logarithmically with increasing frequency
It does not vary with frequency
questions.explanation: An ideal op-amp has infinite gain at every frequency. Real op-amps roll off.

questions.question: What will be the output voltage of the circuit shown in Figure E7-3 if R1 is 1,000 ohms, RF is 10,000 ohms, and 0.23 volts DC is applied to the input?
questions.explanation: Vout = −(RF/R1) × Vin = −(10,000/1,000) × 0.23 = −2.3 V. The inverting configuration flips the sign.

questions.question: What absolute voltage gain can be expected from the circuit in Figure E7-3 when R1 is 1,800 ohms and RF is 68 kilohms?
What absolute voltage gain can be expected from the circuit in Figure E7-3 when R1 is 3,300 ohms and RF is 47 kilohms?
What is an operational amplifier?
answers: A high-gain, direct-coupled differential amplifier with very high input impedance and very low output impedance
A digital audio amplifier whose characteristics are determined by components external to the amplifier
An amplifier used to increase the average output of frequency modulated amateur signals to the legal limit
A RF amplifier used in the UHF and microwave regions
questions.explanation: An op-amp is a high-gain, DC-coupled differential amplifier with very high input impedance and very low output impedance. Its circuit behavior is set by external feedback.

questions.question: What are three common oscillator circuits?
questions.explanation: Colpitts (capacitive divider feedback), Hartley (tapped coil) and Pierce (crystal) are the classic oscillator circuits.

questions.question: What is a microphonic?
answers: An IC used for amplifying microphone signals
Distortion caused by RF pickup on the microphone cable
Changes in oscillator frequency caused by mechanical vibration
Excess loading of the microphone by an oscillator
questions.explanation: Microphonics are frequency shifts caused by mechanical vibration changing the component spacing or values in an oscillator.

questions.question: What is a phase-locked loop?
answers: An electronic servo loop consisting of a ratio detector, reactance modulator, and voltage-controlled oscillator
An electronic circuit also known as a monostable multivibrator
An electronic servo loop consisting of a phase detector, a low-pass filter, a voltage-controlled oscillator, and a stable reference oscillator
An electronic circuit consisting of a precision push-pull amplifier with a differential phase input
questions.explanation: A PLL compares the VCO, divided down, with a stable reference in a phase detector. The low-pass filtered error voltage steers the VCO into lock.

questions.question: How is positive feedback supplied in a Colpitts oscillator?
questions.explanation: A Colpitts oscillator takes its feedback from a capacitive voltage divider across the tank.

questions.question: How is positive feedback supplied in a Pierce oscillator?
questions.explanation: In a Pierce oscillator the quartz crystal itself provides the feedback path between output and input.

questions.question: Which of these functions can be performed by a phase-locked loop?
answers: Wide-band AF and RF power amplification
Comparison of two digital input signals and digital pulse counting
questions.explanation: PLLs synthesize frequencies (VCO plus divider) and can demodulate FM, since the VCO control voltage tracks the input frequency.

questions.question: How can an oscillator’s microphonic responses be reduced?
answers: Reduce noise on the oscillator’s power supply
Mechanically isolate the oscillator circuitry from its enclosure
questions.explanation: Mechanically isolating or shock-mounting the oscillator keeps vibration from reaching frequency-determining parts.

questions.question: Which of the following components can be used to reduce thermal drift in crystal oscillators?
questions.explanation: NP0 (C0G) capacitors have an almost zero temperature coefficient, which minimizes thermal drift.

questions.question: What type of frequency synthesizer circuit uses a phase accumulator, lookup table, digital-to-analog converter, and a low-pass anti-alias filter?
questions.explanation: A DDS uses a phase accumulator to index a waveform lookup table, a DAC to produce analog samples, and a low-pass filter to remove images.

questions.question: What information is contained in the lookup table of a direct digital synthesizer (DDS)?
answers: The phase relationship between a reference oscillator and the output waveform
Amplitude values that represent the desired waveform
The phase relationship between a voltage-controlled oscillator and the output waveform
Frequently used receiver and transmitter frequencies
questions.explanation: The DDS lookup table holds amplitude samples of the waveform (usually a sine) for each phase value.

questions.question: What are the major spectral impurity components of direct digital synthesizers?
questions.explanation: DDS output contains discrete spurs from phase truncation, DAC nonlinearity and quantization, rather than broadband noise.

questions.question: Which of the following ensures that a crystal oscillator operates on the frequency specified by the crystal manufacturer?
answers: Provide the crystal with a specified parallel inductance
Provide the crystal with a specified parallel capacitance
Bias the crystal at a specified voltage
Bias the crystal at a specified current
questions.explanation: Parallel-resonant crystals are calibrated for a specific load (parallel) capacitance. Providing that capacitance puts the oscillator on the marked frequency.

questions.question: Which of the following is a technique for providing highly accurate and stable oscillators needed for microwave transmission and reception?
answers: Use a rubidium stabilized reference oscillator
Use a temperature-controlled high Q dielectric resonator
questions.explanation: GPS-disciplined oscillators, rubidium standards and temperature-controlled high-Q dielectric resonators are all used for stable microwave references. All the choices are correct.

questions.question: What technique shows that a square wave is made up of a sine wave and its odd harmonics?
questions.explanation: Fourier analysis breaks a periodic waveform into sine components. An ideal square wave is the fundamental plus odd harmonics with amplitudes falling as 1/n.

questions.question: Which of the following is a type of analog-to-digital conversion?
questions.explanation: A successive-approximation ADC uses a DAC and a comparator to binary-search for the input value, one bit at a time.

questions.question: Which of the following describes a signal in the time domain?
questions.explanation: A time-domain description shows amplitude versus time, as an oscilloscope does.

questions.question: What is “dither” with respect to analog-to-digital converters?
answers: An abnormal condition where the converter cannot settle on a value to represent the signal
A small amount of noise added to the input signal to reduce quantization noise
An error caused by irregular quantization step size
A method of decimation by randomly skipping samples
questions.explanation: Dither is a small amount of added noise. It randomizes quantization error so the ADC's spurs and distortion are spread out and become less noticeable.

questions.question: What is the benefit of making voltage measurements with a true-RMS calculating meter?
answers: An inverse Fourier transform can be used
The signal’s RMS noise factor is also calculated
The calculated RMS value can be converted directly into phasor form
RMS is measured for both sinusoidal and non-sinusoidal signals
questions.explanation: A true-RMS meter computes the actual RMS value of any waveform. Averaging meters are calibrated only for sine waves.

questions.question: What is the approximate ratio of PEP-to-average power in an unprocessed single-sideband phone signal?
questions.explanation: Unprocessed speech has a high crest factor, so its PEP is roughly 2.5 times the average power.
questions.explanationNote: 2.5:1 is the pool value; real speech varies widely.

questions.question: What determines the PEP-to-average power ratio of an unprocessed single-sideband phone signal?
answers: The frequency of the modulating signal
questions.explanation: Without speech processing, the peak-to-average ratio depends on the characteristics of the speaker's voice.

questions.question: Why are direct or flash conversion analog-to-digital converters used for a software defined radio?
answers: Very low power consumption decreases frequency drift
Immunity to out-of-sequence coding reduces spurious responses
Very high speed allows digitizing high frequencies
questions.explanation: Flash ADCs convert in a single step and are extremely fast, so they can digitize RF directly at high frequencies.

questions.question: How many different input levels can be encoded by an analog-to-digital converter with 8-bit resolution?
answers: 8 multiplied by the gain of the input amplifier
256 divided by the gain of the input amplifier
questions.explanation: An 8-bit converter has 2⁸ = 256 output codes, so it can encode 256 distinct levels.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a low-pass filter used at the output of a digital-to-analog converter?
answers: Lower the input bandwidth to increase the effective resolution
Improve accuracy by removing out-of-sequence codes from the input
Remove spurious sampling artifacts from the output signal
questions.explanation: A DAC's stepped output contains images and sampling artifacts around multiples of the sample rate. A low-pass (reconstruction) filter smooths them out.

questions.question: Which of the following is a measure of the quality of an analog-to-digital converter?
questions.explanation: ADC quality is described by linearity and distortion figures such as THD (along with SINAD and ENOB).

questions.question: What is the modulation index of an FM signal?
answers: The ratio of frequency deviation to modulating signal frequency
The ratio of modulating signal amplitude to frequency deviation
The modulating signal frequency divided by the bandwidth of the transmitted signal
The bandwidth of the transmitted signal divided by the modulating signal frequency
questions.explanation: FM modulation index m = peak deviation ÷ modulating frequency, so it changes as the audio frequency changes.

questions.question: How does the modulation index of a phase-modulated emission vary with RF carrier frequency?
answers: It increases as the RF carrier frequency increases
It decreases as the RF carrier frequency increases
It varies with the square root of the RF carrier frequency
It does not depend on the RF carrier frequency
questions.explanation: In PM, the modulation index is the peak phase deviation, which depends only on the modulating signal and not on the carrier frequency.

questions.question: What is the modulation index of an FM phone signal having a maximum frequency deviation of 3000 Hz either side of the carrier frequency if the highest modulating frequency is 1000 Hz?
What is the modulation index of an FM phone signal having a maximum carrier deviation of plus or minus 6 kHz if the highest modulating frequency  is 2 kHz?
questions.explanation: m = 6 kHz / 2 kHz = 3.

questions.question: What is the deviation ratio of an FM phone signal having a maximum frequency swing of plus or minus 5 kHz if the highest modulation frequency is 3 kHz?
questions.explanation: Deviation ratio = max deviation ÷ max modulating frequency = 5 / 3 ≈ 1.67.

questions.question: What is the deviation ratio of an FM phone signal having a maximum frequency swing of plus or minus 7.5 kHz if the highest modulation frequency is 3.5 kHz?
Orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) is a technique used for which types of amateur communication?
answers: OFDM signals are not allowed on amateur bands
questions.explanation: OFDM is used by amateur digital modes (for example VARA, DRM digital voice and SSTV, and Wi-Fi-based mesh).

questions.question: What describes orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM)?
answers: A frequency modulation technique that uses non-harmonically related frequencies
A bandwidth compression technique using Fourier transforms
A digital mode for narrow-band, slow-speed transmissions
A digital modulation technique using subcarriers at frequencies chosen to avoid intersymbol interference
questions.explanation: OFDM sends data on many closely spaced, mathematically orthogonal subcarriers. Each one runs at a low symbol rate, which resists intersymbol interference from multipath.

questions.question: What is deviation ratio?
answers: The ratio of the audio modulating frequency to the center carrier frequency
The ratio of the maximum carrier frequency deviation to the highest audio modulating frequency
The ratio of the carrier center frequency to the audio modulating frequency
The ratio of the highest audio modulating frequency to the average audio modulating frequency
questions.explanation: Deviation ratio = maximum carrier deviation ÷ highest audio modulating frequency. It is the system-level counterpart of the modulation index.

questions.question: What is frequency division multiplexing (FDM)?
answers: The transmitted signal jumps from band to band at a predetermined rate
Dividing the transmitted signal into separate frequency bands that each carry a different data stream
The transmitted signal is divided into packets of information
Two or more information streams are merged into a digital combiner, which then pulse position modulates the transmitter
questions.explanation: FDM divides the channel into separate frequency sub-bands, each carrying its own data stream.

questions.question: What is digital time division multiplexing?
answers: Two or more data streams are assigned to discrete sub-carriers on an FM transmitter
Two or more signals are arranged to share discrete time slots of a data transmission
Two or more data streams share the same channel by transmitting time of transmission as the sub-carrier
Two or more signals are quadrature modulated to increase bandwidth efficiency
questions.explanation: TDM gives each signal its own recurring time slot on a shared channel. DMR's two time slots are an example.

questions.question: What is Quadrature Amplitude Modulation or QAM?
answers: A technique for digital data compression used in digital television which removes redundancy in the data by comparing bit amplitudes
Transmission of data by modulating the amplitude of two carriers of the same frequency but 90 degrees out of phase
A method of performing single sideband modulation by shifting the phase of the carrier and modulation components of the signal
A technique for analog modulation of television video signals using phase modulation and compression
questions.explanation: QAM amplitude-modulates two carriers of the same frequency in quadrature (90° apart, I and Q). Together they set both amplitude and phase.

questions.question: What is the definition of symbol rate in a digital transmission?
answers: The number of control characters in a message packet
The maximum rate at which the forward error correction code can make corrections
The rate at which the waveform changes to convey information
The number of characters carried per second by the station-to-station link
questions.explanation: Symbol rate (baud) is how many times per second the waveform changes state to carry information. Each symbol may carry several bits.

questions.question: Why should the phase of a PSK signal be changed at the zero crossing of the RF signal?
questions.explanation: Shifting phase when the RF is at zero amplitude avoids abrupt amplitude jumps, which keeps the spectrum narrow.

questions.question: What technique minimizes the bandwidth of a PSK31 signal?
questions.explanation: PSK31 shapes its pulses with a raised-cosine (sinusoidal) envelope, so the amplitude falls to zero smoothly at phase reversals. That keeps the bandwidth to about 31 Hz.

questions.question: What is the approximate bandwidth of a 13-WPM International Morse Code transmission?
questions.explanation: CW bandwidth ≈ WPM × 4 Hz, so 13 × 4 = 52 Hz. This follows from a dot rate of WPM/1.2 Hz with a shaping factor.

questions.question: What is the bandwidth of an FT8 signal?
questions.explanation: FT8 uses 8 tones spaced 6.25 Hz apart, about 50 Hz in total.

questions.question: What is the bandwidth of a 4,800-Hz frequency shift, 9,600-baud ASCII FM transmission?
How does ARQ accomplish error correction?
answers: Special binary codes provide automatic correction
Special polynomial codes provide automatic correction
If errors are detected, redundant data is substituted
If errors are detected, a retransmission is requested
questions.explanation: ARQ (automatic repeat request) detects errors and asks the sender to retransmit the bad block.

questions.question: Which digital code allows only one bit to change between sequential code values?
answers: Extended Binary Coded Decimal Interchange Code
questions.explanation: Gray code changes only one bit between successive values, which avoids glitches in encoders and constellation mapping.

questions.question: How can data rate be increased without increasing bandwidth?
answers: Using a more efficient digital code
questions.explanation: A more efficient code or modulation that carries more bits per symbol raises throughput without widening the signal.

questions.question: What is the relationship between symbol rate and baud?
answers: Baud is twice the symbol rate
Baud rate is half the symbol rate
The relationship depends on the specific code used
questions.explanation: Baud is the symbol rate. The two terms mean the same thing.

questions.question: What factors affect the bandwidth of a transmitted CW signal?
answers: Keying speed and shape factor (rise and fall time)
questions.explanation: Faster keying and sharper rise and fall times both widen a CW signal's spectrum.

questions.question: What is described by the constellation diagram of a QAM or QPSK signal?
answers: How many carriers may be present at the same time
The possible phase and amplitude states for each symbol
Frequency response of the signal stream
The number of bits used for error correction in the protocol
questions.explanation: A constellation diagram plots each allowed symbol as a point in the I/Q plane, showing every possible amplitude-and-phase state.

questions.question: What type of addresses do nodes have in a mesh network?
questions.explanation: Mesh nodes (for example AREDN) are addressed with IP addresses and route standard IP traffic.

questions.question: What technique do individual nodes use to form a mesh network?
answers: Forward error correction and Viterbi codes
Custom code plugs for the local trunking systems
questions.explanation: Mesh nodes find their neighbors with discovery protocols and set up routes automatically (for example OLSR or Babel).

questions.question: Why are received spread spectrum signals resistant to interference?
answers: Signals not using the spread spectrum algorithm are suppressed in the receiver
The high power used by a spread spectrum transmitter keeps its signal from being easily overpowered
Built-in error correction codes minimize interference
If the receiver detects interference, it will signal the transmitter to change frequencies
questions.explanation: The receiver despreads using the same code or hop pattern. Signals that don't match the code stay spread out and are suppressed.

questions.question: What spread spectrum communications technique uses a high-speed binary bit stream to shift the phase of an RF carrier?
questions.explanation: Direct-sequence spread spectrum uses a fast pseudorandom chip stream to phase-modulate (shift) the carrier, spreading it over a wide band.

questions.question: Which describes spread spectrum frequency hopping?
answers: If interference is detected by the receiver, it will signal the transmitter to change frequencies
RF signals are clipped to generate a wide band of harmonics which provides redundancy to correct errors
A binary bit stream is used to shift the phase of an RF carrier very rapidly in a pseudorandom sequence
Rapidly varying the frequency of a transmitted signal according to a pseudorandom sequence
questions.explanation: Frequency hopping moves the carrier quickly among many frequencies in a pseudorandom sequence that the receiver follows.

questions.question: What is the primary effect of extremely short rise or fall time on a CW signal?
questions.explanation: Abrupt keying edges create wide sidebands, heard as key clicks on nearby frequencies.

questions.question: What is the most common method of reducing key clicks?
answers: Increase keying waveform rise and fall times
Insert low-pass filters at the transmitter output
Reduce keying waveform rise and fall times
Insert high-pass filters at the transmitter output
questions.explanation: Slower rise and fall times (about 5 ms, shaped) narrow the spectrum and eliminate key clicks.

questions.question: What is the advantage of including parity bits in ASCII characters?
answers: A larger character set is available
Some types of errors can be detected
questions.explanation: A parity bit makes the count of 1s even or odd, so a single-bit (odd-number) error can be detected. It cannot be corrected.

questions.question: What is a common cause of overmodulation of AFSK signals?
questions.explanation: Driving the transmitter's audio input too hard overmodulates AFSK, causing ALC action and distortion.

questions.question: What parameter evaluates distortion of an AFSK signal caused by excessive input audio levels?
questions.explanation: Excessive audio drive shows up as IMD, which PSK software measures on an idling signal.

questions.question: What is considered an acceptable maximum IMD level for an idling PSK signal?
questions.explanation: A clean PSK31 signal shows IMD of −30 dB or better. Higher values mean overdrive and splatter.

questions.question: What are some of the differences between the Baudot digital code and ASCII?
answers: Baudot uses 4 data bits per character, ASCII uses 7 or 8; Baudot uses 1 character as a letters/figures shift code, ASCII has no letters/figures code
Baudot uses 5 data bits per character, ASCII uses 7 or 8; Baudot uses 2 characters as letters/figures shift codes, ASCII has no letters/figures shift code
Baudot uses 6 data bits per character, ASCII uses 7 or 8; Baudot has no letters/figures shift code, ASCII uses 2 letters/figures shift codes
Baudot uses 7 data bits per character, ASCII uses 8; Baudot has no letters/figures shift code, ASCII uses 2 letters/figures shift codes
questions.explanation: Baudot (ITA2) uses 5 bits and needs LTRS/FIGS shift codes. ASCII uses 7 bits (8 with parity or extended) and needs no shift codes.

questions.question: What is one advantage of using ASCII code for data communications?
answers: It includes built-in error correction features
It contains fewer information bits per character than any other code
It is possible to transmit both uppercase and lowercase text
It uses one character as a shift code to send numeric and special characters
questions.explanation: ASCII has separate codes for uppercase and lowercase letters. Baudot is uppercase only.

questions.question: What is an isotropic radiator?
answers: A calibrated, unidirectional antenna used to make precise antenna gain measurements
An omnidirectional, horizontally polarized, precisely calibrated antenna used to make field measurements of antenna gain
A hypothetical, lossless antenna having equal radiation intensity in all directions used as a reference for antenna gain
A spacecraft antenna used to direct signals toward Earth
questions.explanation: An isotropic radiator is a theoretical lossless point source radiating equally in all directions. It is the 0 dBi reference for antenna gain.

questions.question: What is the effective radiated power (ERP) of a repeater station with 150 watts transmitter power output, 2 dB feed line loss, 2.2 dB duplexer loss, and 7 dBd antenna gain?
questions.explanation: Net gain = 7 − 2 − 2.2 = +2.8 dB. ERP = 150 W × 10^(2.8/10) ≈ 150 × 1.905 ≈ 286 W. ERP is referenced to a dipole, which suits a dBd antenna gain.

questions.question: What term describing total radiated power takes into account all gains and losses?
questions.explanation: ERP is transmitter power with all system gains and losses applied (feed line, duplexer, antenna gain), referenced to a dipole.

questions.question: Which of the following factors affect the feed point impedance of an antenna?
answers: The settings of an antenna tuner at the transmitter
questions.explanation: Antenna height changes how the ground reflection couples back to the antenna, which changes its feed-point impedance. Feed line length and tuner settings don't change the antenna's own impedance.

questions.question: What does the term “ground gain” mean?
answers: The change in signal strength caused by grounding the antenna
The gain of the antenna with respect to a dipole at ground level
To force net gain to 0 dB by grounding part of the antenna
An increase in signal strength from ground reflections in the environment of the antenna
questions.explanation: Ground gain is the extra signal strength at some elevation angles when the direct wave and the ground-reflected wave add in phase.

questions.question: What is the effective radiated power (ERP) of a repeater station with 200 watts transmitter power output, 4 dB feed line loss, 3.2 dB duplexer loss, 0.8 dB circulator loss, and 10 dBd antenna gain?

What is the effective isotropic radiated power (EIRP) of a repeater station with 200 watts transmitter power output, 2 dB feed line loss, 2.8 dB duplexer loss, 1.2 dB circulator loss, and 7 dBi antenna gain?
questions.explanation: Net = 7 − 2 − 2.8 − 1.2 = +1 dB. EIRP = 200 × 10^0.1 ≈ 200 × 1.259 ≈ 252 W. EIRP is the right term because the antenna gain is in dBi.

questions.question: Which frequency band has the smallest first Fresnel zone?
questions.explanation: The Fresnel zone radius scales with √λ, so the highest frequency (5.8 GHz, shortest wavelength) has the smallest first Fresnel zone.

questions.question: What is antenna efficiency?
answers: Radiation resistance divided by transmission resistance
Radiation resistance divided by total resistance
Total resistance divided by radiation resistance
Effective radiated power divided by transmitter output
questions.explanation: Efficiency = Rrad / (Rrad + Rloss), the fraction of input power actually radiated.

questions.question: Which of the following improves the efficiency of a ground-mounted quarter-wave vertical antenna?
answers: Isolating the coax shield from ground
questions.explanation: Radials give the return current a low-loss path. Otherwise it flows through lossy soil, so radials greatly improve a ground-mounted vertical's efficiency.

questions.question: Which of the following determines ground losses for a ground-mounted vertical antenna operating on HF?
questions.explanation: The return current of a ground-mounted vertical flows through the soil, so soil conductivity sets the ground losses (unless an extensive radial field is used).

questions.question: How much gain does an antenna have compared to a half-wavelength dipole if it has 6 dB gain over an isotropic radiator?
questions.explanation: A dipole has 2.15 dBi of gain, so 6 dBi − 2.15 = 3.85 dBd.

questions.question: What is the 3 dB beamwidth of the antenna radiation pattern shown in Figure E9-1?
questions.explanation: In Figure E9-1 the main lobe drops 3 dB at about ±25° from its peak at 0°, so the half-power beamwidth is about 50°.
questions.explanationNote: Figure reading per pool key.

questions.question: What is the front-to-back ratio of the antenna radiation pattern shown in Figure E9-1?
questions.explanation: The main lobe peaks at 0 dB. The rear lobe at 180° reaches about −18 dB, so the front-to-back ratio is about 18 dB.
questions.explanationNote: Figure reading per pool key.

questions.question: What is the front-to-side ratio of the antenna radiation pattern shown in Figure E9-1?
questions.explanation: The response toward the sides (±90°) is about −14 dB, so the front-to-side ratio is about 14 dB.
questions.explanationNote: Figure reading per pool key.

questions.question: What is the front-to-back ratio of the radiation pattern shown in Figure E92?
questions.explanation: In Figure E9-2 the main lobe is the 0 dB reference. The response toward the rear (low angles toward 180°) is about −28 dB, so F/B ≈ 28 dB.
questions.explanationNote: Figure reading per pool key; note the question text references Figure E9-2 (written 'E92' in the pool).

questions.question: What type of antenna pattern is shown in Figure E9-2?
questions.explanation: Figure E9-2 plots response against elevation angle above real ground, from 0° to 180° across the sky. That is an elevation pattern.

questions.question: What is the elevation angle of peak response in the antenna radiation pattern shown in Figure E9-2?
questions.explanation: The strongest lobe in Figure E9-2 peaks just above the horizon, at about 7.5° elevation.

questions.question: What is the difference in radiated power between a lossless antenna with gain and an isotropic radiator driven by the same power?
answers: The power radiated from the directional antenna is increased by the gain of the antenna
The power radiated from the directional antenna is stronger by its front-to-back ratio
The power radiated from the isotropic radiator is 2.15 dB greater than that from the directional antenna
questions.explanation: A lossless antenna radiates all the power fed to it, whatever its pattern. Gain only concentrates that power in some directions.

questions.question: What is the far field of an antenna?
answers: The region of the ionosphere where radiated power is not refracted
The region where radiated power dissipates over a specified time period
The region where radiated field strengths are constant
The region where the shape of the radiation pattern no longer varies with distance
questions.explanation: In the far field, the shape of the pattern no longer changes with distance. Only the field strength keeps falling as 1/r.

questions.question: What type of analysis is commonly used for modeling antennas?
answers: Calculus differentiation with respect to physical properties
questions.explanation: Antenna modeling programs (NEC, EZNEC, MMANA) use the Method of Moments.

questions.question: What is the principle of a Method of Moments analysis?
answers: A wire is modeled as a series of segments, each having a uniform value of current
A wire is modeled as a single sine-wave current generator
A wire is modeled as a single sine-wave voltage source
A wire is modeled as a series of segments, each having a distinct value of voltage across it
questions.explanation: The Method of Moments divides wires into short segments, each assumed to carry a uniform current, and solves for those currents.

questions.question: What is a disadvantage of decreasing the number of wire segments in an antenna model below 10 segments per half-wavelength?
answers: Ground conductivity will not be accurately modeled
The resulting design will favor radiation of harmonic energy
The computed feed point impedance may be incorrect
The antenna will become mechanically unstable
questions.explanation: With too few segments per half-wave the current distribution isn't modeled accurately. Results such as feed-point impedance become unreliable.

questions.question: What type of radiation pattern is created by two 1/4-wavelength vertical antennas spaced 1/2-wavelength apart and fed 180 degrees out of phase?
answers: A figure-eight broadside to the axis of the array
A figure-eight oriented along the axis of the array
questions.explanation: Fed 180° apart with λ/2 spacing, the fields add along the line of the elements and cancel broadside. The result is an end-fire figure-eight.

questions.question: What type of radiation pattern is created by two 1/4-wavelength vertical antennas spaced 1/4-wavelength apart and fed 90 degrees out of phase?
answers: A figure-eight end-fire along the axis of the array
A figure-eight broadside to the axis of the array
questions.explanation: With λ/4 spacing and 90° phasing, the fields reinforce in one direction and cancel in the other, giving a unidirectional cardioid.

questions.question: What type of radiation pattern is created by two 1/4-wavelength vertical antennas spaced 1/2-wavelength apart and fed in phase?
answers: A figure-eight broadside to the axis of the array
A figure-eight end-fire along the axis of the array
questions.explanation: Fed in phase with λ/2 spacing, the fields add broadside and cancel along the axis, giving a broadside figure-eight.

questions.question: What happens to the radiation pattern of an unterminated long wire antenna as the wire length is increased?
answers: Fewer lobes form with the major lobes increasing closer to broadside to the wire
Additional lobes form with major lobes increasingly aligned with the axis of the antenna
The elevation angle increases, and the front-to-rear ratio decreases
The elevation angle increases, while the front-to-rear ratio is unaffected
questions.explanation: As a long wire gets longer it develops more lobes, and the main lobes move closer to the wire's axis.

questions.question: What is the purpose of feeding an off-center-fed dipole (OCFD) between the center and one end instead of at the midpoint?
answers: To create a similar feed point impedance on multiple bands
To suppress off-center lobes at higher frequencies
To resonate the antenna across a wider range of frequencies
To reduce common-mode current coupling on the feed line shield
questions.explanation: Feeding about 1/3 of the way from one end gives a similar impedance (around 200–300 Ω) on several harmonically related bands, so one balun can match them all.

questions.question: What is the effect of adding a terminating resistor to a rhombic or long-wire antenna?
answers: It reflects the standing waves on the antenna elements back to the transmitter
It changes the radiation pattern from bidirectional to unidirectional
It changes the radiation pattern from horizontal to vertical polarization
questions.explanation: A terminating resistor absorbs the forward wave instead of reflecting it, so there's no backward-traveling wave. The pattern becomes unidirectional.

questions.question: What is the approximate feed point impedance at the center of a two-wire half-wave folded dipole antenna?
questions.explanation: A two-wire folded dipole multiplies the dipole impedance by 4: about 4 × 73 ≈ 300 Ω.

questions.question: What is a folded dipole antenna?
answers: A center-fed dipole with the ends folded down 90 degrees at the midpoint of each side
A half-wave dipole with an additional parallel wire connecting its two ends
A dipole configured to provide forward gain
questions.explanation: A folded dipole is a half-wave dipole plus a second parallel conductor joining its ends, forming a narrow loop fed in the middle of one side.

questions.question: Which of the following describes a G5RV antenna?
answers: A wire antenna center-fed through a specific length of open-wire line connected to a balun and coaxial feed line
A phased array antenna consisting of multiple loops
A wide band dipole using shorted coaxial cable for the radiating elements and fed with a 4:1 balun
questions.explanation: A G5RV is a center-fed wire (about 102 ft) fed through a specific length of open-wire or ladder line that transitions to coax, often via a balun.

questions.question: Which of the following describes a Zepp antenna?
answers: A horizontal array capable of quickly changing the direction of maximum radiation by changing phasing lines
An omni-directional antenna commonly used for satellite communications
A vertical array capable of quickly changing the direction of maximum radiation by changing phasing lines
questions.explanation: The original Zepp is an end-fed half-wave dipole, fed through open-wire line at its high-impedance end.

questions.question: How is the far-field elevation pattern of a vertically polarized antenna affected by being mounted over seawater versus soil?
answers: Additional lobes appear at higher elevation angles
Separate elevation lobes will combine into a single lobe
questions.explanation: Seawater is an excellent conductor, so ground reflections are strong and in phase at low angles. Low-angle vertical radiation increases a lot.

questions.question: Which of the following describes an extended double Zepp antenna?
questions.explanation: An extended double Zepp is a center-fed dipole about 1.25 λ long. It is the longest center-fed length that keeps a broadside main lobe with extra gain (about 3 dB over a dipole).

questions.question: How does the radiation pattern of a horizontally polarized antenna vary with increasing height above ground?
answers: The takeoff angle of the lowest elevation lobe increases
The takeoff angle of the lowest elevation lobe decreases
questions.explanation: Raising a horizontal antenna lowers the takeoff angle of its lowest elevation lobe, which favors DX.

questions.question: How does the radiation pattern of a horizontally-polarized antenna mounted above a long slope compare with the same antenna mounted above flat ground?
answers: The main lobe takeoff angle increases in the downhill direction
The main lobe takeoff angle decreases in the downhill direction
The horizontal beamwidth decreases in the downhill direction
The horizontal beamwidth increases in the uphill direction
questions.explanation: Over ground that falls away, the effective height is greater in the downhill direction, so the main lobe's takeoff angle drops that way.

questions.question: How much does the gain of an ideal parabolic reflector antenna increase when the operating frequency is doubled?
questions.explanation: Dish gain ∝ (πD/λ)². Doubling the frequency halves λ, which multiplies the gain by 4, or about 6 dB.

questions.question: How can two linearly polarized Yagi antennas be used to produce circular polarization?
answers: Stack two Yagis to form an array with the respective elements in parallel planes fed 90 degrees out of phase
Stack two Yagis to form an array with the respective elements in parallel planes fed in phase
Arrange two Yagis on the same axis and perpendicular to each other with the driven elements at the same point on the boom and fed 90 degrees out of phase
Arrange two Yagis collinear to each other with the driven elements fed 180 degrees out of phase
questions.explanation: Two crossed Yagis (elements perpendicular) on one boom, with their driven elements at the same point and fed 90° apart, produce circular polarization.

questions.question: What is the most efficient location for a loading coil on an electrically short whip?
answers: Near the center of the vertical radiator
As low as possible on the vertical radiator
questions.explanation: A loading coil near the middle of a short whip keeps the current high in the lower half, raising the radiation resistance, while the coil's losses stay reasonable. That makes it the most efficient location.
questions.explanationNote: Loading-coil placement rationale summarized; pool key says 'near the center'.

questions.question: Why should antenna loading coils have a high ratio of reactance to resistance?
questions.explanation: A high X/R ratio means high coil Q and low loss resistance, so less power is wasted in the coil.

questions.question: Approximately how long is a Yagi’s driven element?
questions.explanation: A Yagi's driven element is a resonant half-wave dipole, about λ/2 long.

questions.question: What happens to SWR bandwidth when one or more loading coils are used to resonate an electrically short antenna?
answers: It is unchanged if the loading coil is located at the feed point
It is unchanged if the loading coil is located at a voltage maximum point
questions.explanation: Loading a short antenna raises its Q, so the SWR bandwidth gets narrower.

questions.question: What is an advantage of top loading an electrically short HF vertical antenna?
questions.explanation: Top loading (a capacitance hat) keeps the current high along the vertical section, which raises the radiation resistance and the efficiency.

questions.question: What happens as the Q of an antenna increases?
answers: More common-mode current is present on the feed line
questions.explanation: Bandwidth ≈ f/Q, so higher antenna Q means narrower SWR bandwidth.

questions.question: What is the function of a loading coil in an electrically short antenna?
answers: To increase the SWR bandwidth by increasing net reactance
To resonate the antenna by cancelling the capacitive reactance
questions.explanation: A short antenna looks capacitive. The loading coil adds inductive reactance to cancel it and bring the antenna to resonance.

questions.question: How does radiation resistance of a base-fed whip antenna change below its resonant frequency?
answers: Radiation resistance does not depend on frequency
questions.explanation: As a whip gets electrically shorter (operated below resonance), its radiation resistance falls sharply, roughly with the square of its electrical length.

questions.question: Why do most two-element Yagis with normal spacing have a reflector instead of a director?
questions.explanation: With normal spacing, a driven element plus reflector gives a bit more gain than a driven element plus director.

questions.question: What is the purpose of making a Yagi’s parasitic elements either longer or shorter than resonance?
questions.explanation: Detuning a parasitic element changes the phase of its induced current. That phase decides whether it acts as a reflector (long, inductive) or a director (short, capacitive).

questions.question: Which matching system for Yagi antennas requires the driven element to be insulated from the boom?
questions.explanation: Beta and hairpin matches connect across a split driven element, whose two halves must be insulated from the boom. Gamma and T matches can be used with an element grounded to the boom at its center.

questions.question: What antenna matching system matches coaxial cable to an antenna by connecting the shield to the center of the antenna and the conductor a fraction of a wavelength to one side?
questions.explanation: A gamma match connects the coax shield to the element's center (its voltage null). The center conductor goes through a series capacitor to a rod that taps the element some distance out, where the impedance is higher.

questions.question: What matching system uses a short length of transmission line connected in parallel with the feed line at or near the feed point?
questions.explanation: A stub match places a short length of line, open or shorted, in parallel with the feed line at a chosen point. Its reactance cancels the reactance there.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the series capacitor in a gamma match?
answers: To provide DC isolation between the feed line and the antenna
To provide a rejection notch that prevents the radiation of harmonics
To transform the antenna impedance to a higher value
questions.explanation: The gamma rod adds inductance. The series capacitor cancels that inductive reactance so the feed point looks resistive.

questions.question: What Yagi driven element feed point impedance is required to use a beta or hairpin matching system?
answers: Capacitive (driven element electrically shorter than 1/2 wavelength)
Inductive (driven element electrically longer than 1/2 wavelength)
questions.explanation: A hairpin is a shunt inductor, so it needs a driven element that is slightly short, with a capacitive feed point. Together they form an L-network that steps up to 50 Ω.

questions.question: Which of these transmission line impedances would be suitable for constructing a quarter-wave Q-section for matching a 100-ohm feed point impedance to a 50-ohm transmission line?
questions.explanation: A quarter-wave transformer needs Z0 = √(Zin × Zload) = √(50 × 100) ≈ 70.7 Ω, and 75 Ω coax is the closest choice.

questions.question: What parameter describes the interaction of a load and transmission line?
questions.explanation: The reflection coefficient Γ = (ZL − Z0)/(ZL + Z0) describes how a load and a line interact (how much is reflected). SWR follows from it.

questions.question: What is a use for a Wilkinson divider?
answers: To divide the operating frequency of a transmitter signal so it can be used on a lower frequency band
To feed high-impedance antennas from a low-impedance source
To divide power equally between two 50-ohm loads while maintaining 50-ohm input impedance
To divide the frequency of the input to a counter to increase its frequency range
questions.explanation: A Wilkinson divider splits power equally into two matched 50 Ω outputs, with isolation between them, while keeping a 50 Ω input.

questions.question: Which of the following is used to shunt feed a grounded tower at its base?
questions.explanation: A grounded tower can be shunt-fed with a gamma match: a wire tapped up the tower with a series capacitor.

questions.question: What is the purpose of using multiple driven elements connected through phasing lines?
answers: To control the antenna’s radiation pattern
To prevent harmonic radiation from the transmitter
To allow single-band antennas to operate on other bands
To create a low-angle radiation pattern
questions.explanation: Phasing lines set the relative amplitude and phase between driven elements, which shapes and steers the radiation pattern.

questions.question: What is the velocity factor of a transmission line?
answers: The ratio of its characteristic impedance to its termination impedance
The ratio of its termination impedance to its characteristic impedance
The velocity of a wave in the transmission line multiplied by the velocity of light in a vacuum
The velocity of a wave in the transmission line divided by the velocity of light in a vacuum
questions.explanation: Velocity factor = wave speed in the line ÷ c, the speed of light in a vacuum.

questions.question: Which of the following has the biggest effect on the velocity factor of a transmission line?
questions.explanation: VF ≈ 1/√εr, so the dielectric material between the conductors largely determines it.

questions.question: Why is the electrical length of a coaxial cable longer than its physical length?
answers: Skin effect is less pronounced in the coaxial cable
Skin effect is more pronounced in the coaxial cable
Electromagnetic waves move faster in coaxial cable than in air
Electromagnetic waves move more slowly in a coaxial cable than in air
questions.explanation: Waves travel more slowly in coax, VF ≈ 0.66–0.85, so a given physical length contains more wavelengths and is electrically longer.

questions.question: What impedance does a 1/2-wavelength transmission line present to an RF generator when the line is shorted at the far end?
answers: The same as the characteristic impedance of the line
The same as the output impedance of the RF generator
questions.explanation: A half-wave line repeats its load impedance at the input. A short at the far end therefore looks like a short (very low impedance) at the generator.

questions.question: What is microstrip?
answers: Special shielding material designed for microwave frequencies
Miniature coax used for low power applications
Short lengths of coax mounted on printed circuit boards to minimize time delay between microwave circuits
Precision printed circuit conductors above a ground plane that provide constant impedance interconnects at microwave frequencies
questions.explanation: Microstrip is a precise PCB trace over a ground plane, forming a controlled-impedance line for microwave interconnects.

questions.question: What is the approximate physical length of an air-insulated, parallel conductor transmission line that is electrically 1/2 wavelength long at 14.10 MHz?
questions.explanation: λ/2 in free space = 150/14.1 MHz ≈ 10.64 m. Air-insulated line has a velocity factor close to 1, so the physical length is about 10.6 m.

questions.question: How does parallel conductor transmission line compare to coaxial cable with a plastic dielectric?
questions.explanation: Open-wire (parallel conductor) line has mostly air as its dielectric and low conductor losses, so it loses much less than plastic-dielectric coax.

questions.question: Which of the following is a significant difference between foam dielectric coaxial cable and solid dielectric coaxial cable, assuming all other parameters are the same?
answers: Foam dielectric coaxial cable has lower safe maximum operating voltage
Foam dielectric coaxial cable has lower loss per unit of length
Foam dielectric coaxial cable has higher velocity factor
questions.explanation: Foam coax has a higher velocity factor and lower loss, but less dielectric strength, so a lower maximum voltage. All the choices are correct.

questions.question: What impedance does a 1/4-wavelength transmission line present to an RF generator when the line is shorted at the far end?
answers: The same as the characteristic impedance of the transmission line
The same as the generator output impedance
questions.explanation: A quarter-wave line inverts impedance, so a short at the far end appears as an open (very high impedance) at the input.

questions.question: What impedance does a 1/8-wavelength transmission line present to an RF generator when the line is shorted at the far end?
answers: The same as the characteristic impedance of the line
questions.explanation: A shorted line less than λ/4 long looks inductive. At λ/8 the input impedance is +jZ0.

questions.question: What impedance does a 1/8-wavelength transmission line present to an RF generator when the line is open at the far end?
answers: The same as the characteristic impedance of the line
questions.explanation: An open line less than λ/4 long looks capacitive. At λ/8 the input impedance is −jZ0.

questions.question: What impedance does a 1/4-wavelength transmission line present to an RF generator when the line is open at the far end?
answers: The same as the characteristic impedance of the line
The same as the input impedance to the generator
questions.explanation: A quarter-wave line inverts impedance, so an open at the far end appears as a short (very low impedance) at the input.

questions.question: Which of the following can be calculated using a Smith chart?
questions.explanation: A Smith chart solves transmission-line problems graphically. In particular it shows how impedance changes with distance along a line.

questions.question: What type of coordinate system is used in a Smith chart?
questions.explanation: The Smith chart is built from constant-resistance circles and constant-reactance arcs.

questions.question: Which of the following is often determined using a Smith chart?
answers: Impedance and SWR values in transmission lines
Point-to-point propagation reliability as a function of frequency
questions.explanation: The Smith chart is used to find impedance and SWR at points along transmission lines.

questions.question: What are the two families of circles and arcs that make up a Smith chart?
questions.explanation: Its two families are constant-resistance circles and constant-reactance arcs.

questions.question: Which of the following is a common use for a Smith chart?
answers: Determine the length and position of an impedance matching stub
Determine the impedance of a transmission line, given the physical dimensions
Determine the gain of an antenna given the physical and electrical parameters
Determine the loss/100 feet of a transmission line, given the velocity factor and conductor materials
questions.explanation: A classic Smith chart use is finding the length and position of a matching stub.

questions.question: On the Smith chart shown in Figure E9-3, what is the name for the large outer circle on which the reactance arcs terminate?
questions.explanation: Per the pool, the outer circle where the reactance arcs end is called the reactance axis. It is the boundary where R = 0, i.e. pure reactance.
questions.explanationNote: Pool calls the outer circle the 'reactance axis'; explanation follows the key.

questions.question: On the Smith chart shown in Figure E9-3, what is the only straight line shown?
questions.explanation: The only straight line on a Smith chart is the horizontal resistance axis (zero reactance), running from a short circuit to an open circuit.

questions.question: How is a Smith chart normalized?
answers: Reassign the reactance axis with resistance values
Reassign the resistance axis with reactance values
Reassign the prime center’s impedance value
Reassign the prime center to the reactance axis
questions.explanation: You normalize by assigning the system impedance (for example 50 Ω) to the prime center and dividing all impedances by it.

questions.question: What third family of circles is often added to a Smith chart during the process of designing impedance matching networks?
questions.explanation: Constant-SWR circles, centered on the prime center, show how impedance moves along a lossless line at a fixed SWR.

questions.question: What do the arcs on a Smith chart represent?
questions.explanation: The arcs are curves of constant reactance, inductive above the resistance axis and capacitive below it.

questions.question: In what units are the wavelength scales on a Smith chart calibrated?
answers: In fractions of transmission line electrical frequency
In fractions of transmission line electrical wavelength
In fractions of antenna electrical wavelength
In fractions of antenna electrical frequency
questions.explanation: The outer scales are in fractions of a wavelength along the line (electrical wavelength), so you can rotate the plotted point by line length.

questions.question: When constructing a Beverage antenna, which of the following factors should be included in the design to achieve good performance at the desired frequency?
answers: Its overall length must not exceed 1/4 wavelength
It must be mounted more than 1 wavelength above ground
It should be configured as a four-sided loop
It should be at least one wavelength long
questions.explanation: A Beverage works as a traveling-wave antenna. It needs to be at least about one wavelength long, at low height, to get useful directivity.

questions.question: Which is generally true for 160- and 80-meter receiving antennas?
answers: Atmospheric noise is so high that directivity is much more important than losses
They must be erected at least 1/2 wavelength above the ground to attain good directivity
Low loss coax transmission line is essential for good performance
questions.explanation: On 160 m and 80 m the atmospheric noise is far above the receiver's noise floor. Directivity, which improves SNR, matters much more than antenna efficiency.

questions.question: What is receiving directivity factor (RDF)?
answers: Forward gain compared to the gain in the reverse direction
Relative directivity compared to a dipole
Peak antenna gain compared to average gain over the hemisphere around and above the antenna
questions.explanation: RDF compares the antenna's peak forward gain with its average gain over the hemisphere around and above it. It shows how well the antenna favors the signal over noise from all directions.

questions.question: What is the purpose of placing an electrostatic shield around a small-loop direction-finding antenna?
answers: It adds capacitive loading, increasing the bandwidth of the antenna
It eliminates unbalanced capacitive coupling to the antenna’s surroundings, improving the depth of its nulls
It eliminates tracking errors caused by strong out-of-band signals
It increases signal strength by providing a better match to the feed line
questions.explanation: An electrostatic shield balances out capacitive coupling to nearby objects (the antenna effect). That keeps the loop's nulls deep and sharp for direction finding.

questions.question: What challenge is presented by a small wire-loop antenna for direction finding?
answers: It has a bidirectional null pattern
It does not have a clearly defined null
It is practical for use only on VHF and higher bands
questions.explanation: A small loop has two nulls 180° apart, so the bearing is ambiguous unless you add a sense antenna.

questions.question: What indicates the correct value of terminating resistance for a Beverage antenna?
answers: Maximum feed point DC resistance at the center of the desired frequency range
Minimum low-angle front-to-back ratio at the design frequency
Maximum DC current in the terminating resistor
Minimum variation in SWR over the desired frequency range
questions.explanation: When the termination equals the line's characteristic impedance, there are no reflections, so the SWR stays nearly flat across the band.

questions.question: What is the function of a Beverage antenna’s termination resistor?
answers: Absorb signals from the reverse direction
questions.explanation: The termination resistor absorbs signals arriving from the back, which would otherwise reflect, making the Beverage unidirectional.

questions.question: What is the function of a sense antenna?
answers: It modifies the pattern of a DF antenna to provide a null in only one direction
It increases the sensitivity of a DF antenna array
It allows DF antennas to receive signals at different vertical angles
It provides diversity reception that cancels multipath signals
questions.explanation: A sense antenna (usually a vertical) is combined with the loop to make a cardioid with a single null, which resolves the 180° ambiguity.

questions.question: What type of radiation pattern is created by a single-turn, terminated loop such as a pennant antenna?
questions.explanation: A terminated single-turn loop such as the pennant or flag has a cardioid pattern with one deep rear null.

questions.question: How can the output voltage of a multiple-turn receiving loop antenna be increased?
answers: By reducing the permeability of the loop shield
By utilizing high impedance wire for the coupling loop
By increasing the number of turns and/or the area enclosed by the loop
questions.explanation: Induced voltage is proportional to the number of turns × the loop area (× frequency). More turns or a larger area give more output.

questions.question: What feature of a cardioid pattern antenna makes it useful for direction-finding antennas?
questions.explanation: A cardioid has a single deep null that points to the signal's direction without the two-way ambiguity of a figure-eight.

questions.question: What is the primary function of an external earth connection or ground rod?
answers: Prevent static build up on power lines
Reduce RF current flow between pieces of equipment
Protect breaker panel from power surges
questions.explanation: A ground rod mainly carries lightning energy into the earth. It does little for RF grounding or equipment interconnection.

questions.question: When evaluating RF exposure levels from your station at a neighbor’s home, what must you do?
answers: Ensure signals from your station are less than the controlled maximum permissible exposure (MPE) limits
Ensure signals from your station are less than the uncontrolled maximum permissible exposure (MPE) limits
Ensure signals from your station are less than the controlled maximum permissible emission (MPE) limits
Ensure signals from your station are less than the uncontrolled maximum permissible emission (MPE) limits
questions.explanation: The public, including your neighbors, is not aware of or in control of the exposure. So the stricter uncontrolled (general population) MPE limits apply (47 CFR §1.1310).

questions.question: Over what range of frequencies are the FCC human body RF exposure limits most restrictive?
questions.explanation: Between 30 and 300 MHz the human body absorbs RF most efficiently because of whole-body resonance, so the MPE limits are lowest there.

questions.question: When evaluating a site with multiple transmitters operating at the same time, the operators and licensees of which transmitters are responsible for mitigating over-exposure situations?
answers: Each transmitter that produces 20 percent or more of its MPE limit in areas where the total MPE limit is exceeded
Each transmitter operating with a duty cycle greater than 25 percent
Each transmitter that produces 5 percent or more of its MPE limit in areas where the total MPE limit is exceeded
Each transmitter operating with a duty cycle greater than 50 percent
questions.explanation: At multi-transmitter sites, each transmitter producing 5% or more of its own MPE limit in an area where the total is exceeded shares responsibility (47 CFR §1.1307(b)).

questions.question: What hazard is created by operating at microwave frequencies?
answers: The high gain antennas commonly used can result in high exposure levels
Microwaves are in the frequency range where wave velocity is higher
The extremely high frequency energy can damage the joints of antenna structures
questions.explanation: Microwave dishes and other high-gain antennas concentrate power into narrow beams, which can create dangerous power densities close to the antenna. The radiation is non-ionizing.

questions.question: Why are there separate electric (E) and magnetic (H) MPE limits at frequencies below 300 MHz?
answers: The body reacts to electromagnetic radiation from both the E and H fields
Ground reflections and scattering cause the field strength to vary with location
E field and H field radiation intensity peaks can occur at different locations
questions.explanation: Below 300 MHz you are often in the near field, where E and H do not track each other. The body responds to both, their peaks occur at different places, and reflections make the levels vary from point to point. All the reasons apply.

questions.question: What is meant by “100% tie-off” regarding tower safety?
answers: All loose ropes and guys secured to a fixed structure
At least one lanyard attached to the tower at all times
All tools secured to the climber’s harness
All circuit breakers feeding power to the tower must be tied closed with tape, cable, or ties
questions.explanation: 100% tie-off means a climber is attached to the structure by at least one lanyard at all times, including while moving or repositioning.

questions.question: What does SAR measure?
answers: The rate at which RF energy is absorbed by the body
The rate of RF energy reflected from stationary terrain
questions.explanation: SAR (specific absorption rate, in W/kg) is the rate at which body tissue absorbs RF energy.

questions.question: Which of the following types of equipment are exempt from RF exposure evaluations?
answers: Transceivers with less than 7 watts of RF output
Antennas that radiate only in the near field
Dish antennas less than one meter in diameter
questions.explanation: Per the pool key, hand-held transceivers sold before May 3, 2021 are exempt from the RF exposure evaluation requirement. That is the date the FCC's revised RF exposure rules took effect.
questions.explanationNote: Exemption detail for pre-2021 handhelds reflects the pool answer key; the underlying FCC rule language was not independently verified.

questions.question: When must an RF exposure evaluation be performed on an amateur station operating on 80 meters?
answers: An evaluation must always be performed
When the ERP of the station is less than 10 watts
When the station’s operating mode is CW
When the output power from the transmitter is less than 100 watts
questions.explanation: Since May 3, 2021, the FCC no longer exempts stations by power level and band (47 CFR §1.1307). Every station must be evaluated, though the evaluation may simply show the station meets an exemption threshold.

questions.question: To what should lanyards be attached while climbing?
questions.explanation: Attach lanyards to the tower legs, the strongest members. Rungs, guy brackets and masts may not hold fall-arrest loads.

questions.question: Where should a shock-absorbing lanyard be attached to a tower when working above ground?
answers: To the belt of the fall-arrest harness
To the next lowest set of guys
questions.explanation: Anchoring a shock-absorbing lanyard above head level limits how far you fall before it arrests you, which reduces the impact force.
